maintopic: WELCOME TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON HIS RETURN FOLLOWING ILLNESS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WELCOME TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON HIS RETURN FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the applause in which we have all joined will express to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) more eloquently than anything I can say how happy we are to see him back with us today and how gratified we are to see with our own eyes that this period of rest has restored him completely to his usual good health and his accustomed robust vigour.
On the first sitting day of this session of parliament I had the privilege of expressing, on behalf of all members of the house, our genuine feeling of sorrow that the hon. gentleman was prevented by illness from being with us at that time. Similarly today I think I express the feelings of all members of the house when I say that this is a happy occasion, and that we all rejoice that he was persuaded to take this necessary rest after the serious illness which overtook him some weeks ago.
We all realize the onerous nature of the responsibilities which fall upon the Leader of the Opposition under our parliamentary system. We all know of the hon. gentleman's strong sense of duty. We all realize that it must have been distressing to him to be obliged to be away from this house during that period. However, we all feel that he was wise in accepting the advice of his medical advisers. I can assure him that our respect for him has been increased by the way he carried out what was recommended as best to enable him to recover his usual good health and vigour in order to be able to discharge the duties of that high office.
It is not too frequently that we have the opportunity of expressing views that are genuinely unanimous in all quarters of the house, but this is one of those occasions. I can assure the hon. gentleman that we were gratified from time to time by the good news we heard of his progress toward complete recovery, and perhaps on no occasion more so than when the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) informed us on that
first sitting day that he had seen the hon. gentleman the previous day and could give us the assurance that the progress he was making was highly satisfactory. That was something that rejoiced us.
We are all now happy to see that the good wishes we asked Your Honour to convey to the hon. gentleman on that day have been fully realized, and to know that that period will probably be only a disagreeable memory. There may perhaps be some compensation in the fact that the hon. gentleman's illness gave us who feel honoured by his personal friendship the opportunity to express publicly our esteem for him and our admiration for the way in which he responds to his sense of duty to the public service.
Once again I can say, with the deep conviction that I am expressing the genuine feeling of every member of the house no matter where he sits, that we extend to the hon. gentleman our very best wishes and our hope, based upon what we see with our own eyes today, that he has fully recovered his health.

maintopic: WELCOME TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON HIS RETURN FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has spoken for all members of the house, may I be pardoned for just adding a word because I did not do so when the hon. gentleman's absence through illness was first referred to. I want to say that we are extremely glad to see him here. No doubt we shall hear that he is as well as he looks. Some people might think the House of Commons has been a more comfortable place during his absence. I am inclined to think that it will be a much more lively place now that he is back again.
On behalf of those associated with me and, I know, all other members of the house, I certainly join in saying how glad we are to see him back. The Prime Minister expressed our sentiments so well that I think there is nothing more for me to say.

maintopic: WELCOME TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON HIS RETURN FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the leader of this group, who happens to be indisposed today, I wish to add to the remarks of the Prime Minister and the leader of the C.C.F. the sentiments of the group which sits in this corner on the occasion of the return to this house of the Leader of the Opposition.

House of Commons
I think all members of parliament and individuals regard their responsibilities with some seriousness, but I have often thought the leaders of the various parties in the house have added responsibilities that sometimes must weigh quite heavily upon them. While very often we do not think alike, and we talk differently, and sometimes arguments in the house become pretty hot and heavy, yet when it is all boiled down I know that each and every one of us has a very high regard for his fellow members. On this occasion it gives us pleasure indeed to welcome back to the house the leader of the official opposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: WELCOME TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON HIS RETURN FOLLOWING ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many ways this is the most momentous occasion I have experienced since I entered this house. The words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those uttered in support of what he said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) have touched me more than I can say. As the Prime Minister remarked, the occasions when unanimity can be expressed in the house are, under our democratic system, not so frequent. If I can assume that there is that measure of unanimity that has been indicated, certainly this is one of the happiest days of my life. I go so far as to say that I confidently feel that the sentiments that have been expressed in this way come from the hearts of members on both sides of the house.
From the time I was so unexpectedly taken out of circulation I have received consideration, kindness, messages of encouragement and those things that help to while away the rather lengthy hours in hospital not only from the members of my own party but from members in every part of the house. The letters I received will always be deeply impressed on my mind, because it was surprising to find the warmth of expression that came from so many where perhaps it might be least expected.
It was not only from members of the house that I received encouragement of this kind, but from people all over Canada. I received convincing evidence that those of us in the house who are performing public service to the best of our ability, no matter to what party we belong, are in the minds of the people of Canada, and that perhaps we are not so critically, regarded as sometimes may be thought. I received so many letters that I will always cherish, but I can hardly refrain from mentioning the fact that nearly every letter I received mentioned that not only the wishes but the prayers of those writing were with me.
I think one of the most deeply moving letters I received was from a boy of 11 whom

I have never met, but now that I have returned I intend to meet him. He wrote to me and said, "Dear Mr. Drew: I am writing to you because I also had meningitis. While I was in hospital my mother and father prayed for me and I know what prayers mean. I just want you to know that I am praying for you because I know how lonely it is in hospital." I need not tell you that when my wife read that letter to me in the hospital there were tears in our eyes. But that, I thought, was encouraging in more than a personal way because it did indicate exactly the extent to which so many people are concerned about the activities that we carry on here.
In expressing my appreciation to the members of the house it would be less than fitting if I did not express my very great appreciation to a friend of many long years, the Hon. Earl Rowe, who has carried on in my absence. Sometimes I do not obey orders very well. I am afraid my wife would be the first witness to that. But on this occasion I have done so, and actually until my return here he was the only member I saw because my instructions were to remove myself from political activities and the hurly-burly of the affairs that go on here. He performed the task-and I have naturally followed his performance in the daily press

with great ability, and with the devotion that for so many years he has shown to the public life of this country.
I know he would be the first to say that he would not wish to be singled out, because I recognize that, with him, I owe a very great debt of gratitude to the members of my party for the way in which they have carried on and assumed the burdens that my illness placed upon them. To all of them I am naturally deeply grateful, but to every one of you I wish to express my profound thanks for the kindness and courtesy you have shown. This is the first time during the numerous years I have served in municipal councils, a provincial legislature and here at Ottawa that I have been away for more than a few days, and I come back with a greater appreciation than ever before of what the House of Commons means and of what our associations in the House of Commons mean to every one of us.
May I say that the remarks made by the Prime Minister at the opening of the session and conveyed to me through you, Mr. Speaker, signalized that understanding that exists between all of us that under our system it is possible for us to respect the different

opinions we may hold about public affairs and retain warm personal friendships at the same time. There may be times when, ' jokingly or otherwise, some will say they would be glad to see me perhaps not quite so active as I have been, and remarks of that kind may be made quite naturally in the heat of debate on both sides of the house; but what the Prime Minister and other members have said today and what you have all conveyed in your many messages of sympathy and understanding is an expression of the great privilege we all have of serving in a parliament where there is freedom to disagree without any suggestion that we are imputing improper motives to those who hold different opinions from our own.
I cannot help but recall one letter in particular that I received from one of the ministers sitting opposite who, in wishing me good luck, said; "Do get back as soon as you can so you can lambaste us as vigorously as ever." Well, in case any of you might think the kindness that has been extended has muzzled me, I say this is one occasion on which I shall, without reservation, accept the advice that has been given from the other side.
May I, in expressing appreciation not only for the kindness and the advice, say with deep sincerity how grateful I am to the members of the press gallery for the consideration they have shown during the period that I have been away. It might not have been unnatural to have assumed very gloomy prospects for the outcome of my illness, but instead of that there has been kindness, consideration and a genuine expression of friendly good will which has helped very much in the very gratifying recovery that I have had from the illness from which I suffered. Perhaps just before I close these remarks I might say that I have had very convincing evidence of the excellence of our medical services here in Canada, and of the importance of these new and benign drugs that now mean so much to the health of all our people.
Again, Mr. Speaker, to you who extended on behalf of the members of the house the very generous resolution adopted here some time ago, and also to you personally as well as your wife for the flowers you were good enough to send to my wife and myself, and to every member in this house, may I simply say from the bottom of my heart, thank you every one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The Department of National Health and Welfare has control over the use of new insecticides under the Food and Drugs Act which specifies that food shall not be adulterated. In addition, the department acts in a technical advisory capacity to the Department of Agriculture with respect to administration of the health section of the Pest Control Products Act, assisting the administrators of the act in ensuring that insecticides registered under the act shall carry adequate

Data submitted by the manufacturer in support of claims made as to the safety with which products can be used is reviewed by specialist members of the committee and spot checking of validity of data is carried out in the government's laboratories. In its three years of operation, the committee has dealt with over 200 insecticidal products.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON TESTS OF BELGIAN RIFLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. In view of this week's debate at Westminster, can the minister give the house a report as to the tests carried out in Canada on the Belgian FN rifle?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON TESTS OF BELGIAN RIFLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. While we have not reached a final decision on the adoption of the FN rifle, the Canadian army, as hon. members probably know, has been carrying out a series of extensive field trials which have given very encouraging results. We expect these tests will be completed in about two months.
In the meantime, production drawings have been converted from the metric to the inch system, and production details have been brought into line with North American practices. In other words we are taking such steps as we can, without making a major financial commitment, to prepare for the production of the rifle at an early date, if it is adopted.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: TELEVISION
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR RELAY STATION AT THREE RIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question. I have had it translated so I can understand it.
The first part deals with whether or not representations have been received relative to the installation by the C.B.C. of a T.V. relay station in the Three Rivers area. The answer is, of course, that we have had representations of that type made to us.
With reference to whether or not the C.B.C. is prepared to do anything about it, I might say that the present licensing policy of the C.B.C. would permit a licence for a private applicant in that particular area.
These relay stations are what are more commonly known in the trade as booster stations. They are not yet available, and these lower priced transmitters are not being built; but if a plan were developed requiring

But we would point out that in some places companies are being organized to establish good reception points and link them by wire to television receivers. This, however, is a private endeavour, and the C.B.C. has not participated in it. However, this matter is under constant study, and if or when we change policy with respect to it I shall make that known to the house.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT WITH RESPECT TO BITTER POTATOES
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Because of last year's wet season and the unusual quantity of bitter potatoes grown, and since such potatoes may result in toxic poisoning, what action if any has the Department of National Health and Welfare taken to warn the general public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ACTION BY GOVERNMENT WITH RESPECT TO BITTER POTATOES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
gave me notice of his question the day before yesterday. In reply I may say that potatoes that are bitter are green in colour and may contain solanine. This solanine is an alkaloid and is normally present in potatoes in very small amounts. Unusual growing conditions may increase the amount of solanine to a dangerous level. Poisoning from the consumption of these potatoes has been reported, and this is being investigated.
If there are known to be any green potatoes or potatoes from which people have suffered illness, the matter should be reported either to the local food and drug inspector, or to the head office in Ottawa. Action will then be taken to have the dangerous material removed from the market and destroyed.

In view of the definite steps being taken by the United Kingdom to set up atomic power plants, will the minister comment on press reports which suggest that squabbles in the United States are having the effect of delaying action on Canada's extremely important peacetime atomic power program?

Inquiries of the Ministry Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce): I can say definitely that no squabble in the United States is delaying the Canadian program. The Canadian program is being pressed forward actively, but Canada is in a little different position from the United Kingdom in that the cost of coal in this country is considerably less than in the United Kingdom, and we feel that we should not attempt to develop atomic power that will not be competitive in cost with power produced from coal. I expect the time is not far distant when we shall be able to announce a program to the House of Commons, but I am not ready to do it today.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Before I begin my remarks I should like to be sure, sir, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) would not like to take advantage of this occasion to

start lambasting the government right away, because if he would I should be only too happy to yield.
I shall have ample opportunity at a later occasion to take advantage of the offer.

Mr. Speaker, since this will probably be the last non-controversial thing I shall say in the next little while, perhaps, as the first speaker in the debate since the Leader of the Opposition returned to the house I might echo the feeling of pleasure that all of us have in seeing him back here, and echo also-perhaps there may be a little more controversy about this-the view expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that the house will be a livelier place now that the Leader of the Opposition is back here. If I may use a phrase which was once used in this house, and say it in a kindly way, I hope I shall not be misunderstood if I say that I think we now all understand better the fable that, in the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
That fell with a thud.
Explain.
The minister had better stick to being a straight man.

When the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) moved the vote of want of confidence in the government to which I am now replying he stated-I am not reading his exact words, but I think I am paraphrasing them exactly-that parliament year in and year out has had no chance to debate immigration; and he placed the blame for that circumstance on my predecessor, the present Minister of Finance. He stated, rather inaccurately, that over the years the present Minister of Finance had the responsibility for arranging the debates in this house.
As hon. members know, of course, that statement is not correct except for the first session of this parliament. Until that time the present Minister of Finance had no more responsibility for arranging the debates than any other member of the government. It seems to me it is perfectly obvious whose fault it is that the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration came at the end of the session, virtually every session.
On purpose.

If there is any doubt about that, there cannot be any doubt that it would have been just as easy for the opposition, had they wanted to do so, to bring on a debate such as the one we are having now
Immigration
at any time in any previous session. Every session there have to be from ten to a dozen motions to go into supply, and when such motions are made it is open to any hon. member to move the kind of motion the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) now has before the house.
If there had been any real desire on the part of the opposition to have an early debate on immigration last year or the year before or the year before that it would have been perfectly easy for them to have had it on a supply motion.
Not only that, but last year 16 days or about 68 hours were consumed in the debate on the address. That was the first time I was present in the house when that debate took place. Practically every conceivable subject was discussed, and it would have been quite easy to have had a discussion on immigration at that time.
So I think all this time that has been taken in suggesting that there has been no opportunity in previous sessions to discuss immigration is a real waste of the time of parliament. I suggest that the real reason the Department of Citizenship and Immigration came up late in previous sessions was that members of the opposition knew very well that under my predecessor that department was well administered and there was no particular reason to bring on a debate.
I know that there is a very simple and obvious retort to that. I think perhaps the reason this subject has been brought up early in the present session is that the opposition feel that having a comparative novice as minister in place of a very experienced minister there may be more opportunity to make political capital this year than there was in previous sessions. The motion moved by the hon. member reads:
in the opinion of this house, the immigration policy of the government is not clear, consistent or co-ordinated; is not in conformity with the needs or the responsibilities of Canada; and in its administration denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike.
There are three parts to that motion, and for obvious reasons I am going to deal with them in reverse order. I am going to deal first with the charge, and it is a charge, that the administration of the department denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike. The hon. member for Kamloops in making his case for this proposition raised two points, and only two points, in support of it. He said there was a so-called mess in the department revealed at the bar meeting in Winnipeg. He said further that the department had ignored the decision of

Immigration
the Supreme Court of Canada in the Leong Ba Chai case and that that was evidence of the denial of justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike.
I should like first to deal with the incident chat arose in Winnipeg. I may say that a number of hon. members on the other side expressed some surprise that I did not speak early in the debate. The principal reason I did not speak was that I had expected the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) to speak on this subject. So far as I know the hon. member for Prince Albert was the only member of this house who was actually present at the bar meeting in Winnipeg, at least he is the only member of whose presence I am aware.
I was there too.

The hon. member for
Prince Albert made his presence felt by certain utterances which found their way, correctly or incorrectly, into the press and one of which I have right here with me now. The hon. member for Prince Albert made a speech at Teulon, Manitoba, a place that both he and I had occasion to visit during the latter part of last year. On September 3 he was quoted by the Canadian Press, or reported-I want to be accurate about this

as having demanded a royal commission to investigate the activities of Canada's immigration department. The report says that his demand followed charges by the Canadian Bar Association subcommittee of shocking procedural practices in the department's overseas offices.
It seems to me that the hon. member, if he had personal knowledge of those shocking practices, would want to give them to the house and would also want to give the person who had to answer to this house an opportunity of replying to what he had to say. But the hon. gentleman has preferred not to do that. It was indicated to me that he did not intend to speak, at any rate until after I had something to say.
I am not really surprised by this. As a matter of fact, if I may say so without disrespect, I think it is rather characteristic of the hon. member for Prince Albert. I do not think there is an hon. member in this house who is quicker to hitch a lift on any political bandwagon that comes along than is the hon. member for Prince Albert. Of course it just so happens that over the years it has been too bad for him that so many of those conveyances that looked like bandwagons turned out to be political hearses.
If I may try to depict imaginatively what must have occurred or what seems to have

occurred to the hon. member for Prince Albert at Winnipeg, I would imagine that on that occasion he did not think he had found a bandwagon, but one of those three-wheeled war chariots that Queen Boadicea and her troops used to take into battle in the days when the Romans first came to Britain.
Two-wheeled.

They
had knives on the wheels.

The only trouble with this particular war chariot, whether three or twowheeled-this particular war chariot was supposed to have three wheels-is that the hon. member for Prince Albert found that one of the wheels was not there, and he also began to suspect that there were no spokes in the other two wheels. So with characteristic chivalry-
It sounds like your policy.

So with characteristic chivalry the hon. member for Prince Albert handed this broken down chariot over to the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). If I may change my metaphor a little before I mix it, like the Duke of Plazatoro, he preferred to lead his army from behind. I hope some of my colleagues and some of my friends are keeping their eyes on the hon. member for Prince Albert, for I would not be surprised that as night falls and the battle is practically over the hon. member will rush into the fray and try to dispatch any of his opponents who by that time happen to be unarmed.
If, in this debate, the hon. member for Prince Albert has shown more discretion than valour, it seems to me that the hon. member for Kamloops has shown more valour than discretion. But that is not uncharacteristic either. The hon. member for Kamloops demanded the resignation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) because of his alleged failure to clean up the mess in the department over which he formerly presided. This demand as made is reported here in Hansard at page 1166. I do not think I shall bother to read it.
Spell it out.

I do not think I shall
bother to read it unless the hon. gentleman wants me to do so. If he does, inasmuch as I have unlimited time and will have no hesitation about using it, I am quite prepared to do so.
That is about the only weapon you have.

Let us wait and see. The reasons given, of course, for demanding this resignation were that there were these so-called shocking revelations in Winnipeg. When I read-at the time I came back from Newfoundland-about what was going on in Winnipeg, I must say quite frankly that I was a little bit surprised. The first thing I did when I arrived back in Ottawa was to get in touch with my hon. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey). I discovered that he had not been in Winnipeg at all. I do not intend to say anything more about his position in the matter than this. He has in the most honourable way possible dissociated himself from this whole business with which he was not-in so far as there were any charges or anything of that sort-ever concerned. Beyond that I intend to let the hon. gentleman speak for himself as, to the knowledge of every member of the house, he is perfectly capable of doing.
This so-called report that was not acceptable to the Canadian Bar Association and that was sent back for further study I described in a press conference broadcast as being a perfectly innocuous document; and that is what it is. In order that hon. members who have not had the opportunity that I have had to read it may see how absolutely innocuous it is, I propose to read every word of it into the record. The copy I have here-and I am informed this is a copy of the document that was actually presented-is headed:
Canadian Bar Association Committee on civil liberties Subcommittee on immigration A. J. Cowan, Esq., O.B.E., M.C., Q.C.,
Chairman of the civil liberties committee,
Canadian Bar Association.
Dear Sir:
I have the honour to submit the 1953-54 report on the subcommittee-
I am sure this must mean "report of".
-on immigration.
2.	The terms of reference of the subcommittee as established at the 1952 meeting of the association are as follows:-
And this is in quotation marks.
"That a subcommittee on immigration be established to review the administration of immigration laws and regulations with particular reference to the curtailments of the rights of Canadians by immigration authorities and to report to the committee on civil liberties at the next annual meeting, the members of the subcommittee to be appointed by the chairman."
3.	The terms of reference of the subcommittee were further extended for a year at the 1953 meeting of the association and its membership continued to consist of John H. McDonald, of Ottawa, chairman; John H. Dickey, M.P. of Halifax; John R. Taylor, of Vancouver.
4.	Four meetings of the full committee were held in Ottawa and eight other meetings of two members of the committee were held in Ottawa and
Immigration
Montreal. A comprehensive brief was received from the British Columbia section of the Canadian Bar Association. The recommendations made in this report have been considered and are incorporated herein. In addition a great deal of valuable research work was undertaken by John R. Taylor, a member of the committee. Mr. Taylor has reviewed over two hundred specific cases and has written four comprehensive reports on administrative procedures. These reports have been invaluable to the subcommittee and will form the basis for further study and representations. Copies of these reports are being filed with the chairman of the committee on civil liberties. However, the committee and particularly Mr. Taylor, the author, believe that until such time as the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has had an opportunity of reviewing the detailed material contained in these reports, they should not be generally distributed.
5.	In its 1953 report, the committee recommended certain administrative reforms within the Department of Citizenship and Immigration itself and the creation of an immigration appeal board based on a judicial and legal concept.
6.	A copy of the 1953 report (P. 162 Vol. 36, C.B.A. proceedings) -
I have that in my hand, but I am not going to waste the time of the house in reading it unless someone asks me to do so, because it is the same kind of thing.
-was forwarded to the minister of citizenship and immigration and on June 30, 1954, the committee attended upon the minister and further recommended :
(a)	Possible codification of regulations issued by your department.
(b)	Publications of intradepartmental directives -particularly instructions to field officers as to the application of interpretation of the act.
(c)	The implementation of proper and legal appeal procedures as contemplated in the act and as recommended in this subcommittee's preliminary report last year.
(d)	The possibility of making departmental files available to applicants and their attorneys- possibly as handled by the patent office. (Excluding confidential material prepared and written by departmental officials but including all statements made by the appellant or any other person pertaining to the case).
(e)	The recognition of the role of barristers and solicitors in immigration law.
(f) The establishment of a procedure setting forth reasons for rejection in each case, in such a way as to give the rejected party or the applicant concerned an opportunity of overcoming the department's objections.
(g)	The committee's recommendations made in the 1953 report be implemented.
7.	On July 1, 1954, the then minister of citizenship and immigration, the Hon. Walter Harris, became Minister of Finance and the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill became Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. However, the latter has been absent from Ottawa throughout the summer-
I plead guilty to that charge, Mr. Speaker; I was in Newfoundland.
-and indicated that he would request his predecessor, who has since July 1, 1954, been acting minister of citizenship and immigration, to continue to deal with this matter and the acting minister agreed to so do.
8.	Subsequently, at Mr. Harris' request, conversations were held with the deputy minister of citizenship and immigration. He indicated that the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the

Immigration
Hon. J. W. Pickersgill would appreciate the opportunity of reviewing the several recommendations of the subcommittee. The deputy minister also indicated that he would attend the thirty-sixth annual meeting of the association in Winnipeg and would be available to answer questions regarding immigration procedure which might be raised.
9.	Your subcommittee expresses regret that no action has been taken by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to implement any of the recommendations contained in its 1953 report. We recommend that the subcommittee be continued for a further year, that it be instructed to continue to examine the administration of immigration laws and regulations in accordance with its terms of reference, and to press for action by the department to bring into effect administrative and procedural reforms which will be in accordance with recommendations contained in previous reports of your subcommittee, recommendations in this report, and such further recommendations as may in the future appear to be appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
John H. McDonald, Chairman.
53 Queen Street,
Ottawa,
27th August, 1954.
These are the "shocking revelations". If there is any member of this house who can find any kind of revelation in this document whatsoever, I should like him to make himself known. It is true that there are certain recommendations in it and that most of those recommendations have not been carried out. I do not think they could be carried out by any responsible person administering the act. But there is nothing in that document which, by any stretch of the imagination, can be called a revelation.
I know that something else happened at Winnipeg. I am quite well aware of that fact and I am not going to shirk dealing with it. The hon. member for Kamloops apparently agrees with me that this report is innocuous, because he really did not base his case on the report at all. He based his case on a newspaper report of a speech which was supposed to have been made by Mr. John H. McDonald, and on the unpublished summary of some cases which had been investigated, I presume, by Mr. Taylor. Now, Mr. McDonald is a politician. He is in fact a Liberal politician.
A bad one, too.

And I am one of those Liberals who, contrary to the views that seem to be held on the other side of the house, think even Liberals can make mistakes, and sometimes do. Moreover, I am a politician and a novice at politics, but I do know that it is an occupational hazard of politicians to make speeches, and ill-considered speeches at times. I do not think any member of the house with comparable experience knows that better than the hon. member for Kamloops. I do not think there is anything much more

to be said about Mr. McDonald's speech. At any rate, the contents, so far as I saw them reported in the newspapers, did not amount to much more than that. As to the summary prepared by Mr. Taylor-
May I ask the minister a question?
Yes.
Surely I am correct in assuming that Mr. McDonald has never modified or retracted anything he is reported to have said in that press conference?

I really cannot say, sir. I have not attempted to find out. I come now to the summary of Mr. Taylor's cases, if indeed it was a summary of Mr. Taylor's cases, to which the hon. member for Kamloops referred. He did not identify his document and he did not quote from it either, I admit, but he said he had seen it. I have seen a document which I am informed was prepared by Mr. Taylor and which I assume is the same one. At any rate, I have read a summary of these cases which are supposed to reveal the shocking practices in the department. I would not care at all if it were published anywhere at any time, because I am sure most hon. members on both sides of the house, if they read it, would have the same impression I had. That was the impression that Mr. Taylor had been acting as an advocate before the department for a number of clients, that he had not been uniformly successful in his advocacy, and he did not like it.
All of us have that kind of experience at times, and if any hon. member wants to bring this document to the committee on estimates or anywhere else and discuss it in detail I am perfectly prepared to discuss it at any time I am given a few hours in which to refresh my memory as to the individual cases, because obviously I could not possibly carry the details in my mind.

I do not like to interrupt, but I think perhaps on a question of privilege I should point out that I did not confine my criticism nor the cases I drew to the attention of the house to anything that may have been contained in a document alleged to have been prepared by Mr. Taylor. I think in fairness to Mr. Taylor it should be stated that my case does not depend for its justification on anything Mr. Taylor may have said. If it coincides with what Mr. Taylor may have said I am happy, but it was not based upon an alleged document prepared by Mr. Taylor.

Mr. Speaker, I listened pretty carefully the other day to what was

said by the hon. member for Kamloops. I reread, I admit rather hastily, his speech this morning; and I am unable to find, outside of the Ba Chai case, any other cases referred to except those contained in this summary. If it was not Mr. Taylor's summary to which the hon. member referred he will have other opportunities to refer to these cases again, but that is the only one I was able to find.
I think they may be the same or very similar.
I think they probably are similar, almost to the point of identity.
A strange coincidence.

But the hon. member for Kamloops does make a very much more serious charge when he charges that the department ignored a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Leong Ba Chai case. The position of the department and the minister in this case is set out just as briefly as I can set it out in a letter which I sent to Mr. Foon Sien, the president, I believe, of the Chinese benevolent association in Vancouver. As the letter was intended for publication if he wished to publish it, I think the simplest way I can inform the house of the position of the department and myself in this matter is to read the letter. It was written on the 30th December and reads:
Dear Mr. Foon Sien:
I duly received your letter of December 7, concerning the case of Leong Ba Chai. The application of Leong Hung Hing on behalf of Leong Ba Chai had been given consideration shortly after it had been filed on March 6, 1951. The settlement arrangements were found to be satisfactory. The application was refused, however, on the information given by the applicant that Leong Ba Chai was the child of a concubine.
Application was made before the supreme court of British Columbia on March 5,	1952, for a
mandamus directed to the Pacific district superintendent. The Supreme Court of Canada heard this case on December 8 and 9, and rendered its judgment on December 18, 1953.
The Supreme Court of Canada came to the conclusion that article 1065 of the civil code of China provided for legitimation by acknowledgment by the natural father: that where it was established that a child had been legitimated in China while his father had his domicile there, the law of Canada will recognize such child as legitimate within the meaning of order in council P.C. 2115; that, consequently, mandamus will lie directing the immigration officer concerned to determine whether the child otherwise complies with the provisions of the Immigration Act.
The immigration branch therefore proceeded with the application, and dealt with the case as though Leong Ba Chai, stated to be the son of a concubine, were a "child" within the meaning of P.C. 2115. Leong Hung Hing, the applicant, was examined in Vancouver in January, 1954, at which interview his solicitor, Mr. Anderson, was present.
After considering the report of this interview, the immigration superintendent at Hong Kong was
Immigration
requested to proceed with the case of Leong Ba Chai as an applicant for a visa and to interview him as soon as possible. Leong Ba Chai was examined in Hong Kong on April 22 and April 29. The reports were received in Ottawa early in May and in the course of this month the X-rays were studied by the immigration medical officers in Ottawa. The radiological examination could not be completed until further X-ray plates were received and it was not until July 21 that a final report was obtained.
On or about that date the immigration branch was furnished with letters written in Chinese that had been exchanged between Leong Hung Hing and his son. This correspondence, some 20 letters in all, had to be translated and studied in Ottawa. Thereafter, Leong Ba Chai was interviewed further and investigations were conducted in Hong Kong.
The minutes of all the interviews and of the investigations were under study in Ottawa with a view to preparing a complete and final report on this case when the news of the applicant's death reached Ottawa on November 30. Since the applicant has died, it is obvious that Leong Ba Chai cannot now be admitted as the child of a Canadian citizen who is in a position to receive and care for his dependent.
That is one of the most inhuman things I have ever heard of.

May I ask a
question?
Yes.
Did the supreme court and the appeal court of British Columbia give precisely the same decision as the Supreme Court of Canada gave?

I am unable to answer that question. I have not examined any judgment except the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada which, it seemed to me, was the only judgment that was relevant to the administration of the department. Of course in that respect I am in a somewhat better position than the hon. member for Kamloops confessed himself to be on Tuesday, when I asked him the direct question whether he had read the judgment and he admitted that he had not.
No, I did not. I have read the judgment. I said I did not have it here with me.
Would the hon. gentleman like me to read the passage?
Yes.
This is what was said at page 1167 of Hansard for February 15.
Has the hon. member the court's decision there?

No, I have not got the court's decision, but I have discussed it with counsel and I have a summary of it here.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. Any assumption I have made that the hon. gentleman did not read it or any imputation to that effect I withdraw unreservedly, sir.

Immigration
In his speech the hon. member raised what I regard as far and away the most important question that has been raised in this debate. As I want to be completely fair about this, because I think it is quite important that all of us understand it, I am going to ask the house to allow me to read what the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) said. It seems to me this is the nub of the whole matter. If we are going to have any understanding of this very serious charge that the administration of this department denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike, we must know what is the nature of the injustice.
This is what the hon. gentleman indicated himself, and I believe he may even feel I am quoting too much, but I want to get it fully on the record so it is fresh in the minds of all hon. members when I make my reply. I admit this is difficult material, and as the house knows I have a disadvantage in not having the learning of the hon. gentleman.
Which hon. gentleman?
The hon. member for Kamloops; I am not a member of the bar.

That is no handicap. I
thought it was another handicap about which you were talking.

The hon. member for Kamloops said at page 1164 of Hansard for February 15, 1955, in the second column, the last paragraph:
This party-
I presume he means the hon. gentlemen immediately opposite the government.
-is strongly of the view that you cannot base your practice, in a matter as important as this affecting the welfare of hundreds of thousands of Canadians individually as well as of the country generally, on the principle that there is no matter of right but only of discretion. The reason that we say that is that immigration does affect Canadian citizens.
Well, of course it affects Canadian citizens.
Canadian citizens have rights in spite of what this government may feel to the contrary. Under the Immigration Act and regulations there are laid down classes of admissible immigrants. It is provided that Canadian citizens can apply for the admission of relatives within those classes. It is therefore impossible to argue, or at least unrealistic to argue, that where a Canadian citizen applies for the admission of his relative within one of the admissible classes, no matter what may be the racial origin of that Canadian citizen-we are all the same as citizens-
I certainly agree with that sentiment.
-that Canadian citizen has no rights. He has rights. He has a right above all to know, if his relative is refused admission, why that should be.
I have not finished quoting this passage, but I want to make this interjection. I know

that may seem a most reasonable position to take; and when I argue, as I am going to argue, that it is not a proper position to take, then I am asking hon. members to accept a view which their first instinct might not lead them to accept. It is very important, therefore, that we get these things as straight as we possibly can.
I continue quoting from the top of page 1165:
He has a right to have his objections heard if he thinks that his rights have been overruled or disregarded by the departmental decision.
Then I interjected and asked the hon. member this question:
Will the hon. member permit a question? Will he cite the section of the Immigration Act on which he bases the argument he has just made?
The hon. member then went on:
I thought I might get that sort of question from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because he apparently does not believe that Canadian citizens have rights in general.
Of course that is not quite an accurate statement of my position. I know quite well that Canadian citizens have rights in general and rights in particular, and it was the rights in particular about which I was concerned. It was a question whether Canadian citizens had any rights in this particular matter and, if so, what they were. I am not a lawyer, and I do not know where else you would find these rights but in the relevant statute; I may be wrong.
He believes that it is necessary to lay down the rights of Canadian citizens by some statute before they have any rights.
In general, sir, when we are talking about legal rights, and that is all we are talking about here, not moral rights, under our system of government I suppose that is true. There are, as I am sure the hon. member would tell me if I did not interject it, certain common law rights. But apart from that, it seems to me we look to the statutes for these specific, particular rights. Perhaps that is one of the reasons we are here.
We proceed on the basis that a Canadian citizen has rights, one of them being access to the courts. Unless they are taken away from him by statute those rights exist and are capable of enforcement in the courts.
I do not know that that is of particular significance or relevant. Now I go on with what the hon. member for Kamloops had to say:
Therefore, when you say in the first place that immigration to Canada shall be permitted, and you then make a regulation saying that certain classes are admissible and provide that Canadian citizens can apply for the admission of relatives within that class, how can the minister argue that there is no right on the part of the Canadian citizen when he makes an application? That is the

implication of the minister's argument. It is a position which we entirely refute and refuse to accept.
Now, sir, what is the right of these Canadian citizens? What did the supreme court say it was in the Leong Ba Chai case? I feel that the hon. member will agree with me that the law now is what the supreme court says it is, though we may of course change it here if we want to change it.
Or evade it.

I believe if the hon. gentleman would read this judgment again, as I am sure he has already, he would find there is a very simple remedy if it is evaded. I am not going to read the whole of this because I do not think I should try the house by doing so. I feel those passages I am going to read will set out the law.
First of all, the supreme court makes its decision on this point. I understand that the hon. member for Kamloops the other day took exception to my describing the mother of this person as a concubine. Instead, I will say she was the second wife while the first wife was living. At any rate the court had decided that if the alleged father had Chinese domicile at the time the child was born, under Canadian law he would be regarded as legitimate. Here is the relevant part of the judgment after that:
It naturally follows that the applicant, being the legitimate son, under 21 years of age, of a Chinese citizen,-
Now, it does not say of the particular person concerned; it says of a Chinese citizen:
-legally admitted to and resident in Canada, does not fall within the ban of the regulation, but may be admitted to the country, if he otherwise complies with the provisions of the Immigration Act.
In other words he is a person who is in an admissible class, and therefore a Canadian citizen certainly has this right as long as the law remains in its present state. He can apply for the entry of his child. But after the application is made, that person must satisfy all the other requirements that parliament has seen fit to lay down for the admission of an immigrant to Canada before he can be admitted. Then it goes on to say:
It is claimed by the appellants that a writ of mandamus does not lie, and that no order may be issued directing the immigration officer to consider the application for admission of Ba Chai into Canada as an immigrant. With this, I disagree.
And this is the learned judge speaking.
What is asked is not the admission-
Immigration
I would ask those hon. members who are interested to pay particular attention to these next two sentences:
What is asked is not the admission of Ba Chai into Canada, but the consideration of his application which must be examined in the light of the Immigration Act. This has been illegally denied.
As soon as this decision was made the department proceeded to deal with the application. I have already dealt with that matter in the letter I read to the house.
Then the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) raised another point. The second to last sentence of the judgment deals with that point, as to whether proceedings could be taken against an immigration officer if he did not carry out his duty. The learned judge said:
If he refuses to act and discharge that duty, he is amenable to the ordinary process of the courts.
So if the immigration officer did not carry out his duty, the decision of the supreme court has said that he can be haled into court for his failure to do so. So there is certainly a remedy there.
The position, therefore, as this judgment says, is that if a person belongs to an admissible class, as it is described under the Immigration Act or the regulations-one of those classes where it is laid down that a Canadian citizen or a Canadian resident may apply for the admission of that person-it is the duty of the department to process that application and reach a conclusion with respect to it. But nowhere in that judgment is there any suggestion that the judgment of any court should be substituted for the judgment of the responsible minister in the case.
That is true.
That is a position with' which I think the hon. member for Kamloops readily agrees.
I do not agree with the position, but I agree with the minister's interpretation of the judgment. However, I do not agree with the position of the department.

That helps me, because I was going on into a field in which I felt more uncertainty than the field which I am now examining. In the passage I just read the hon. member for Kamloops almost but not quite said that the prospective immigrants themselves had certain rights.
No, I did not say that.

It may be that he did not
say that, exactly; but he said something close to it. Now, the correct position-

Read the passage where I said that.
If the hon. member does not wish to say it now, then that creates an area of agreement between us which I shall be glad to have.
I think the minister should substantiate his point. He has said that I said certain things, and I have asked him to show me where I said them.
I think I said that he almost, but not quite, said it. I think that was precisely the language I used, and I assure the hon. member that if I used any other phrase I shall apologize to him publicly.
More straw men.
As a matter of fact, the reason I ventured to say this was perhaps a somewhat frivolous one, unbecoming to a minister. The hon. member for Kamloops, unlike myself, is a Rhodes scholar.
What's wrong with that?

Well, personally, sir, I do not think that is the greatest of the demerits of the hon. member for Kamloops. But I think the hon. member for Kamloops had better beware when he, a Rhodes scholar, suggests such things as rights that are not conferred by statute, general and unlimited rights. He had better keep a sharp eye on the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), or he will be accused of being a socialist, a centralizer or, even worse, an international banker.
I doubt if the minister has ever heard of Magna Carta. Certainly if he has he pays no attention to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He used to teach history.
He did not produce any Rhodes scholars, though.

And if the hon. member for Kamloops would like to edify the house by explaining the connection between Magna Carta and any possible legal rights an alien might have when entering Canada, I would be most interested to hear that piece of very original historical research.
I can assure the minister that the hon. member for Prince Albert will be instructing the minister in due course on those points-points on which obviously he needs considerable instruction.

I shall await that with interest. It seems to me the correct legal position in this matter-as a matter of fact, the correct position stated in very simple and non-legal language-has been stated by one

who, like me, was not a lawyer. This position was set out by Mr. Mackenzie King on May 1, 1947, in these words:
With regard to the selection of immigrants, much has been said about discrimination. X wish to make it quite clear that Canada is perfectly within her rights in selecting the persons whom we regard as desirable future citizens. It is not a "fundamental human right" of an alien to enter Canada. It is a privilege. It is a matter of domestic policy. Immigration is subject to the control of the parliament of Canada. This does not mean, however, that we should not seek to remove from our legislation discrimination which appears to be objectionable.
The proper legal position was well stated in the house on June 26 of last year by my predecessor, and I should like to read into the record what he said; because at that time the same point had been raised as is raised in this debate by the same hon. member opposite. I imagine the house will be rather more impressed by the opinion of my predecessor, with the experience he has had, than it would be by my opinion. I find this at page 6832 of Hansard for June 26, 1954:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. As the hon. member knows, we discussed this at some length-perhaps not this particular detail, but the over-all theory of immigration-when we were revising the Immigration Act two years ago.
And all but one member of that committee- and I think this was endorsed by the house-held the view that immigration could not possibly become a matter of law, and we did not want to get into the system which obtains in some other countries whereby we would try to define in a law those persons who could be admitted to Canada, so that one could approach the courts in this country and have a judge decide in an action at law whether an applicant came within the terms of the law.
We went into that matter at some length-
The events to which he referred took place before I was a member of the house. I continue:
We went into that matter at some length, and indeed the minister brought it to the attention of the committee, pointing out that the discretion vested in the minister was so extensive that, as the Leader of the Opposition said today,-
That was on June 26 last.
-the power was so great that "even the minister might not wish to exercise it".
Nevertheless the committee did decide that the theory of immigration in Canada must be that the minister would be responsible to parliament to explain the policy in detail, and his administration of it; and if the administration of the act and of the policy did not meet with the approval of hon. members, then the minister would be subjected to such criticism as members felt they should make. It was felt that we could not have these things going through our courts with decisions being made on the law.
Starting from that, it seems to me it would not be possible, nor would it be desirable, for that matter, to disclose to the applicants information which is on the file in this department, and which would lead the minister and those under him to come to a conclusion in a particular case. I did not understand my hon. friend's concluding words,

when he said that hon. members do not have access to these documents. I have never hesitated to offer a file to any member who asked for it-
This is the former minister of citizenship and immigration, and I am only too happy to endorse his words.
I have never hesitated to offer a file to any member who asked for it, always knowing that, under his responsibility as a member of parliament, such member would consider it confidential. Yet at the same time I know the hon. member has in mind cases where, to the applicants, it would seem that if they knew the problem in the mind of the official they could meet such specialized objection by producing new evidence. I shall not attempt to make a joke of a serious matter, but I could say that we have people who come to our office and say, "I am so and so; what do I have to tell you in order to get into Canada?"
Some hon. members may have read the article by Blair Fraser which appeared in a recent issue of Maclean9s magazine about the immigration office at Hong Kong; and this is no joke, as that article clearly shows. I continue:
That is something we do not want to encourage. So that I think we ought to leave it the way it is. I grant you that quite probably members of parliament in particular should be given all the information available to enable them to criticize a minister of the government. But I do not think that we can have an applicant going outside the department and suing in the courts in an attempt to prove his right to enter Canada.
That is, an alien or a non-Canadian.
As I say, the committee decided that should not be done.
Both houses of parliament decided that should not be done, and it is the law that it should not be done.

While the minister is dealing with that point, would he care to deal with the question of the right of the Canadian citizen who has applied for the admission of a relative to go to court to establish the admissibility of the relative, and therefore the necessity of obtaining information as to why he was denied admission?

As I apprehend the law, I think it is perfectly clear that it is the right of the Canadian citizen to apply and to have that application decided by the minister in the final analysis, or by someone under the minister's control; and it is no more than that. That is exactly what the supreme court said it was in the plainest and most unmistakably clear language. If the hon. gentleman wants the act amended, he is a member of parliament just as I am and he can introduce a bill to amend it. If he can convince a majority of hon. members that it should be amended in that way, well, it will be amended. But I suspect that if the hon. gentleman were sitting on the treasury benches he would never introduce such an amendment.
