Immigration
There are one or two other reasons which I want to give the house today, based on my own very limited experience in the department, in addition to these very compelling reasons which were given by the Minister of Finance when he was minister of citizenship and immigration last year. I realize the feeling people have that we ought to tell the Canadian citizen why some relative of his is not admissible under the act. That seems a most reasonable request to make. I am going to suggest that in addition to the reasons given by the minister there are a number of other reasons why this should not be done.
The information we get from an applicant for admission to Canada, the information we ask from anybody who applies to come to Canada, is extensive. We have to ask it because the act requires it, and because parliament decided this information should be asked for. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), who does not appear to be in her seat at the moment, although she was here a little while ago, was quite concerned that we did not ask enough questions of one particular immigrant. The number of questions we have to ask, prying into the private lives of these people, elicits information which I do not believe should ever be given to anybody else, no matter how close a relative he may be. It seems to me it is a serious enough disability for these people to be refused admission to Canada without giving other people, certainly solicitors, advocates and other people who may use the information in a different way, information about the private lives of people who we have decided are not in our opinion likely to be good Canadian citizens.
Hon. members know the kind of information that results in exclusion. For example, there is the question as to whether a person has ever been in an insane asylum, the question of whether there has been any criminal conviction, the question of whether he has had certain diseases.

What
about Banks?

Any time the hon. gentleman wants to make a speech about Mr. Banks and I have the right to reply, I shall be delighted to reply. But his remark is not very relevant to this general argument, this difficult argument that I am attempting to make at the moment.
There is of course, as every hon. member knows, another kind of inquiry that has to be made. Because of the state of the world it is considered desirable by the government, and it seems to be approved by parliament, that we should inquire whether those prospective immigrants are likely to be a danger

Immigration
to the security of the state. The only way information of any value can be obtained in most cases is from sources which are not within the control of the Canadian government. The information is made available to the Canadian government only because we undertake to keep it confidential. It would not be made available if we did not keep it confidential. That is not true in all these cases. In many cases it is a criminal conviction, previous insanity or some other defect in the person's record that is the reason for the refusal. But of course if we isolated all the other reasons and gave all of them, then we would be labelling the remainder as security cases and doing indirectly what we have undertaken not to do directly.
The other reason, which is of some importance, is this. Last year there were over 150,000 immigrants landed in this country. I cannot say, and I do not think anyone can say because you cannot tell when an application really becomes an application, how many persons approached our offices with a view to becoming immigrants, but it must have been three, four or five times that number.
Parliament is willing to vote only a certain amount of money for the administration of the Immigration Act. After all, the purpose of our Immigration Act is to get good immigrants into Canada and not to enter into complicated consideration of marginal cases. It would be utterly impossible to administer the Immigration Act with any funds that I can envisage parliament voting for the purpose if every case concerning a relative of someone in Canada was taken before the courts or before some kind of tribunal. That is a practical reason, but I admit that it is not quite of the same order of importance as the others I have mentioned. However, it is a limiting factor.
On the other hand, some of us have got into the habit of regarding these applications as being something like trials in court. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), while he did not go so far as to say they were trials, did say-I have looked over his words carefully but I do not think I shall read the passage, as I do not think he will quarrel with what I am going to say-or suggest, as reported at page 1170 of Hansard, that these people were being convicted without being heard, and if they could bring evidence a different judgment might be rendered.
I think that we ought to try to clear our minds of this wrong analogy with the courts. These people are not on trial at all in the sense that someone is on trial in a court. They are people who have applied for entry into this country, which we have a perfect

right to deny to anyone who is not a Canadian. I think a far better analogy, one which would make this whole process seem much more sensible and reasonable as it really is, would be an application for a position of trust, an application for membership in a club, an application for credit from a financial institution or, as the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) said in his speech on Tuesday, an application for admission to a family.
That is precisely what it is. These Canadian citizens are asking to have relatives of theirs, some members of their families, admitted into the larger Canadian family. We have to decide in some way or other whether they are suitable persons to admit. Parliament has decided that that must be done administratively and not by tribunals. If it is to be done administratively the final decision must rest with someone who is answerable to parliament here in parliament.
The hon. member for Kamloops admitted that immigration should be selective. He used that word, and I do not think there are many in his party who would quarrel with it. I think the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) came pretty close to saying that we should open the doors to anybody who wanted to come in, although at the same time he did not seem to be very much in favour of allowing anybody in. I do not want to be unfair to the hon. gentleman, and I would not really suggest that seriously as a summary of his speech, which did rather confuse me.
The hon. member for Kamloops admitted that immigration should be selective. I am one of those old-fashioned people like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell), who like to look up the definition of words in a dictionary before he uses them. The hon. member in another context wanted to read me the definition of a word I had used in this house. I would have been only too happy to have had that done. I must say that I do not understand there is any real difference between the words selection and discrimination. They both mean the same thing.
They sound different.

As the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) says, they sound different. That is quite correct; they do sound different. Mr. Mackenzie King used to look in the dictionary and he was also a little old-fashioned. He used words accurately in his statement of May, 1947, when he said:
This does not mean, however, that we should not seek to remove from our legislation what may appear to be objectionable discrimination.

One of the features of our legislation to which strong objection has been taken on the ground of discrimination is the Chinese immigration act. This act seems to place persons from one particular country in an inferior category. The government has already initiated action for the repeal of that statute. Chinese residents of Canada who are not already Canadian citizens may now be naturalized. Once naturalized, they are permitted to bring their wives and unmarried children under 18 to join them in this country.
That age limit was later raised by this government to 21 years, and in exceptional cases of merit from 21 to 25 years. I think the house might like to know what has been the result of that policy. I had some statistics prepared the other day covering the period from May 1, 1947, because I anticipated the kind of observations which were made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway the other evening. I felt, as I generally do, pretty sympathetic to anything that was said by the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Kingsway. But I doubt if even he realizes how much has been accomplished under the new policy that was instituted in 1947.
There have been 16,600 new files established in the department since May 1, 1947. That does not mean there were only 16,600 applications, because some of those files related to more than one person. Approximately 15,000 applied to one or more persons. They have been checked, and at the present time the number of rejections is 1,217. I could give a further breakdown but I do not think it would add particularly to the argument at this time. I shall be glad to give that in the estimates committee where I hope to be very soon, if anyone is interested.
The total number of persons of the Chinese race admitted to Canada since May 1, 1947 is 11,404. It will be seen that there has been a considerable number, having regard to the number of persons of Chinese origin already in this country. I think hon. members should be reminded that since this policy was instituted on May 1, 1947, the government on the mainland of China has been supplanted by another government, and that during part of that period troops under the control of that other government were actually engaged in combat with Canadian troops in Korea. During that period the present de facto government of China has participated in this cold war. It must be evident to anyone that to have continued a policy as generous as this one has been in circumstances like that was a most exceptional thing to do. I think the Canadian people are to be commended for their willingness to see a policy of that sort continued during times like those when it might have been very easy to use the argument that for security reasons it should be abandoned.
Immigration
But we cannot abandon those security considerations and it would be wrong to do so. There is no doubt whatsoever that under this arrangement we have, we open the possibility of infiltrating, under the guise of relatives, people who are not relatives at all but who are being insinuated into this country not because any Chinese person in this country is disloyal to Canada but because he may be blackmailed. By people who know much more about these things than I do, I am advised that this is a real risk.
As hon. members know, we take virtually no immigrants from beyond the iron curtain in Europe. In other words, our policy so far as Chinese are concerned, if it is discriminatory, is discriminatory in a sense contrary to that which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) suggested the other day. It is discriminatory in favour of Chinese rather than against them. But be that as it may, security is a really serious problem, particularly in view of the difficulties of getting information and even vital statistics. It is a very difficult problem to carry out any kind of security checks on which reliance can be placed. That is the principal reason why it is necessary in these cases sometimes to take a long time and to go back and check and recheck when the circumstances seem to be extremely suspicious indeed, as they sometimes do in some of these cases.
I think I have said really all I want to say about that particular aspect of the subject, except that I want to express to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway appreciation of his personal vote of confidence in the minister. While we were being denounced by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) the other day because we had all this discretion and because we should not be trusted with it, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway later in the evening, as reported at page 1193 of Hansard, said this:
I believe that a certain discretionary power should be given the minister to deal with cases such as I have mentioned.-
He was there referring to grandchildren of Chinese and other similar cases of merit. -when he thinks the weight of evidence presented to him indicates that certain persons should be allowed to enter the country. I quite appreciate that this is a great deal of power to put in the hands of a minister, but I am sure no minister of immigration would misuse a power of that kind.
We do not share his trust.
I thank the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

Perhaps I should say "not willingly".

Immigration

So far as discrimination is concerned, I am more concerned to see that there is no discrimination as between one person and another who is in this country, who has been admitted to this country, than I am about a certain limited discrimination among those whom we admit.
While I am on this subject, and having referred to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, I appeal to hon. members on both sides of the house; I ask them if it has been their experience that the former minister or, for that matter, the present minister although he has not had much experience, has not on all occasions been willing to look at any kind of evidence that might make it possible for him to reach a more informed decision in these cases.
' The other day the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) said that I was a new minister and, like a new broom, he expected me to sweep the house clean. May I say that I do not believe in superfluous effort. The house that I entered on July 1 had already been swept and was quite clean, and there was no need to sweep it clean. When I suggested that, the hon. member jumped right to the opposite extreme and said, "Of course, the minister thinks everything is perfect". Of course the minister does not think anything of the kind. I am perfectly certain that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) made some mistakes when he was minister of citizenship and immigration.
We certainly share that view.

I am also certain that I have already made mistakes. But I do not believe that my hon. friend made any mistakes that were not honest mistakes of judgment. I do not believe any member of the house would say otherwise. What is more, Mr. Speaker, I have now been the minister of this department for seven months and I must say for the officials-and no one has criticized the officials, or anyone who has appeared to criticize them has said he was not doing so-that I have never encountered more conscientious, hard-working people who try harder to reach a proper judgment in these cases, with a leaning always to humanity but bearing in mind that their first duty in administering the Immigration Act is to get people who will be good Canadians and good citizens. I can say that my highest hope as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will be to do as well as my predecessor has done. I know that I cannot do better.

There is one way in which one may perhaps test his administration in a rough but objective way. During the period when the Minister of Finance was minister of citizenship and immigration, he was responsible for permitting three-quarters of a million human beings to land in this country as immigrants. During that same time he found it necessary to deport fewer than 1,500 persons from among those landed immigrants. I do not think there are many members on either side of the house who think there are many people still in Canada who ought to have been deported. There may be a few. I know the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) thinks there is one-
She is not alone.

-because she says so quite publicly. I think most Canadians feel as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said, and I agree with most of what he said. As he said, I think most of the immigrants who have come to Canada-the vast majority of them- are good people who are going to be good Canadian citizens. I believe most Canadians think so too.
Before going on-
When are you going to stop?

If the hon. gentleman is convinced that he should vote for us and not for the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), I am quite prepared to stop. But if he is not so convinced, I am going to go on trying to convince him.
You are losing votes all the time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I guess we are in for an all-day rain.

It is hard to satisfy some people in this house. I sat silent from 2.30 in the afternoon until ten o'clock at night the other day and was accused of failing in my duty in not enunciating the policy of the government.

You are
doing a lot of squirming.
Well, sir, hon. gentlemen asked for it and they are going to get it.
We have not had it yet.

I realize that this may never happen again in my parliamentary career, but for once I have unlimited time and I am going to make the same kind of use of it that is from time to time made by hon. members on the front benches opposite, but I hope to better effect.
That is your own opinion.
Nothing I am stating is anyone else's opinion. All my opinions are my own.
Thank the Lord for that.
Does not the rest of the cabinet even agree with you?

That is
cabinet solidarity, is it?
Oh, I am going to deal with that too. I am not going to dodge any of these things.
Is the minister not enunciating government policy?

Most assuredly. I have the responsibility in this field for the enunciation of policy. It is not my exclusive function to make the policy but once it is made I speak for the government in this field as long as I remain in the government.
That may not be long.
Do I understand from the minister's remarks that his opinions constitute the policy of the government?

No, sir. I am sure the hon. member is far too intelligent and well instructed not to be able to make a clear distinction between an opinion and a policy. I express opinions on many subjects, sometimes indiscreetly, which are none of my business at all, and being the kind of person I am, I am afraid I am apt to go on doing that.
As I started to say before I was interrupted by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), before going on to deal with the second part of the want of confidence motion I want to deal very briefly-
Good.

-with certain other points regarding the administration of the department. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) suggest, and to find the suggestion echoed in rather mild fashion by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) who talked very good sense most of the time in his speech, that immigrants were treated like cattle or in too military a fashion. I think that is an approximation to the phrase used by the hon. member for Red Deer. I do not think I need to say very much about that because it seemed to me that the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) put the matter pretty well in his reply. But I do want to say that I went to Halifax myself
Immigration
and had the good fortune to be there at a time when an Italian ship arrived. I saw the way that immigrants were treated there. Both the hon. members for Halifax were with me at the time, and I was very proud indeed to be told by the purser of that ship, after the landing of these people had been completed, that among all the places where he had called there was no place where people were treated with the same kind of consideration that they were here in Canada.
Of course some hon. members opposite may think I am biased in this matter, although I personally have almost nothing to do with these things. They are done by the officials of the department and they and the officials of other departments are very like other Canadians. There are a few of them who are objectionable but the great majority of them are very considerate of their fellow men, no matter where they come from. Now, sir, I am not going to read this, if hon. members are getting frightened-
Read it.

-but somebody did send me the day before yesterday a copy of the February 11 issue of the Canada Weekly Review which is published in London by a gentleman named Thomson who, I believe, is not notoriously a supporter of the government. I would commend to any hon. members who might be interested in an article entitled, "Welcome Waiting in Montreal at Busy Immigration Department Headquarters". It is not uncomplimentary.
I do not think the hon. member for Red Deer really meant it as censure of the department but he did raise some question-and I think the matter was raised by one or two other hon. members-that sometimes there was misrepresentation of conditions in Canada by officials of the immigration department abroad. Of course, you know, it is very hard not to have some charges of this sort because this is, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will agree, a matter of opinion up to a point. It is not quite susceptible to purely objective treatment.
Even our officials vary in their views as to what conditions are like in Canada and what is going to happen to an immigrant when he comes here. I may say that one of the first complaints that came to me after I became the minister was that some official of the immigration department in London or somewhere in the United Kingdom had said that conditions in Newfoundland were unsuitable for immigrants. I have been trying to find that official ever since but so far I have not found him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
After all, you are exhibit No. 1.

Immigration
There may be something in what the hon. gentleman says.
More truth than fiction.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) referred to a ship called the Beaverbrae and something that he had heard had happened on the Beaverbrae a number of years ago.
He was not too sure.

I am not too sure there may not have been something in what he said. At any rate, I will be only too happy to have the whole thing investigated. I do not think anything comparable with that is going on at the present time. If there is, I would certainly like to know about it and if I find it I will be the first to admit it. It may well be that the subject is worth investigating, and if the hon. member can give me any particulars to help to investigate it more completely I will be very glad to do it.
I should also like to say a word or two about the questions of relief and health services which were raised by the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White). There is no doubt that it is a difficult problem. Of course, as all hon. members know, it is the policy of the department to provide for unemployed immigrants and their families for the first year they are in Canada, so that the problem does not arise at all during the first year. Then we have agreements for health care with seven of the ten provinces which can extend to as long as two years.
But there is in the act this very controversial provision that a person who becomes a public charge can be deported. I know there is a good deal of feeling on both sides of the house about the wisdom of having that provision in the act. I cannot take it out, but parliament can. I am not absolutely convinced that it would be a wise thing to take it out, although I am not terribly proud of having it there. Hon. members know that one of the reasons why it is there is that it was represented to us that if it were not there then in certain provinces and certain localities the entry of immigrants would be actively discouraged, and that on balance it is apt to make the flow of immigration greater than otherwise. But I must say that of all the things that are in the act it is the thing that I am least happy about, and I confess that quite frankly.
Would the minister permit a question?
Certainly.

I do not know whether the minister has discussed this matter with the
[Mr. Knowles.!
Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), but with respect to people who become unemployed a short time after they have arrived in Canada is there any provision for assistance through the Department of Labour in the nature of unemployment insurance?

No, sir, assistance is given directly by my department for the first year. It is true, I believe, that the Department of Labour had a hostel at Ajax and it has one at St. Paul l'Ermite, but that is an activity that was associated with those large-scale movements with which the Department of Labour was concerned at one time. This activity is diminishing and virtually the whole job is done now by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Of course, no person who becomes unemployed in the first year is ever regarded as being a public charge and deported. It is when that condition arises later on that action is taken.
I am not going to name names or constituencies but I would say, sir, that the only members who have written to me to suggest that any person should be deported because of becoming a public charge were certain hon. members of the official opposition. I think perhaps before the opposition expresses too strong views on this subject they should have a caucus on it. But there again, sir, I am not minding my own business.
I come now to part 2 of the hon. member's motion. If the hon. member wishes to withdraw part 2 and part 1 of his motion, I am quite prepared to sit down right now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Getting tired?

I take it he is not. Part 2 of his motion is to the effect that the immigration policy is not in conformity with the needs or responsibilities of Canada. Now, what are the needs of Canada? The hon. member for Kamloops said that the needs of the country for more people are undisputed. Well, if they are undisputed it would appear that we on this side recognize it just as much as anyone on the other side does. The hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) both said immigration did not adversely affect the prospects for employment. The hon. member for Eglinton paid the department the compliment of reading a lot of departmental literature into the record to show where he had obtained the idea. I am glad there are some people in the country, and in the house, who do share the views held by the department and by the government that immigration, within the absorptive capacity of our economy, does not adversely affect employment but does tend to stimulate employment.

At the same time we do recognize it is desirable, so far as is humanly possible, to time the immigration so that the highest degree of influx coincides with the highest degree of opportunity seasonally for employment, not with the lowest. Most hon. members who commented on this aspect agreed with it.
The only conclusion I could reach after rereading the speech of the hon. member for Kamloops was that this part of his motion was based on one phrase, and not entirely an original phrase. It was the one phrase in his speech which got headlines in one of the newspapers. He talked about the government's planning for a little Canada, and said it was to be strongly condemned. I suppose that means, I do not want to be unfair, that we have not brought in enough immigrants; that there should have been more.
What are the facts? Now, the new post-war immigration policy was inaugurated on May 1, 1947, as I have reminded hon. members several times today. At that date the population of Canada was about 12 million. Seven years later the population of this country is 15 million, a 25 per cent increase. It is true there is an element in those figures that I ought to mention. During that period, at midnight on March 31, 1949, we admitted about a third of a million additional new citizens at one stroke. But even making allowance for the addition of the Newfoundlanders, it is a very rapid rate of growth indeed. I question very much whether it could have been much faster. There may have been periods when it could have been a bit faster, but there have been other periods when it might have been better if, in some categories, it had been slowed down a little sooner. You cannot gauge these things accurately. On the whole, I doubt if there could have been a very much more rapid increase than that.
The hon. member for Kamloops said we were neglecting British immigration. I do not suppose he expected anyone in the house to take that seriously. I imagine that was one of the things all of us sometimes permit ourselves to say for consumption elsewhere than in this house. As the hon. member knows, and as I am sure every hon. member knows, there is no country overseas from which it is easier to come to Canada than the United Kingdom. We have fewer formalities, speedier procedures and many more officers and officials there than anywhere else. We do carry on there what we are unable to do in very many countries, and that is an active promotional campaign. Apparently the campaign is so active that
Immigration
sometimes the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) finds people who feel we are encouraging too many people to come to Canada by telling them it is too attractive a country.
I believe the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) indicated that not only were we doing everything we could to encourage immigration from the United Kingdom, but that we were getting, on the whole, good results.
Then the hon. member for Eglinton came and put on his fiercest bulldog expression, and he barked at the house. When I first came-

He did not
bray.

When I first came to the house, I used to be a little frightened by the hon. gentleman's bark. But when I found that practically all his bark was a commendation of the immigration policy and of the results achieved, I felt all I could do was express appreciation of most of what he said.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe the hon. gentleman has a right to say that a member of this house is barking. I believe that expression should be withdrawn.

If I said anything offensive to anyone, I withdraw it unreservedly.
I want to go on, sir, to the third part of the motion, which is really the first part. I repeat my offer to the hon. member for Kamloops; if he wants to withdraw part 1 of his motion, I will sit down.
I have no intention of withdrawing anything. It is even weightier than I had realized.

Apparently the reason why the immigration policy of the government is not clear, consistent or co-ordinated is that on January 28, I believe it was, in a newspaper-and I did not check these dates -I am supposed to have said one thing at a meeting in Ottawa West, and my right hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is supposed to have said something that differed in some way from what I said. His statement was made at Winnipeg.
Well, now, there is quite a difference between me and the Minister of Agriculture.
But you are both long-winded.

The Minister of Agriculture has been a politician for 40 years, and in all that time he has always expressed himself in a bold and forthright fashion. I, sir,

Immigration
spent 16 years in the shelter of the civil service, and my natural mode of expression is timid and careful.
The fear I expressed the other day at that meeting in Ottawa West was not the fear that our absorptive capacity was declining, because I do not think it is. Rather, the fear I expressed was that it was going to be more difficult to find suitable immigrants to come to Canada than it had been. And that, of course, is true. The economic conditions have improved so greatly in western Europe in the last two years that the economic inducement of people to migrate is very much less than it was.
In consequence of this I recognize, and I think the house must recognize, that it is going to be a good deal more difficult to get the people we would most like to get, because we think they would fit best into the kind of society we have, and the kind we want to continue to have. If that is differing from the Minister of Agriculture, who wants more people to come, then I do not understand differences at all. The Minister of Agriculture may have a more optimistic attitude than I have as to how many people could come in a certain year. Indeed, I think it would be very unlikely that any two members on the treasury bench would agree exactly on a subject of that sort-which, after all, is only a matter of opinion.
But we both agree that Canada can absorb immigrants; and we both agree we want to increase the population of this country through the right kind of immigration. And I do not think any small differences between us amount to a row of pins.
Now, if you want a really clear and forthright detailed blueprint for immigration to this country, here it is! I took the trouble to get a copy of the resolution adopted by the national convention of the Progressive Conservative party on September 30 and October 1 and 2 of 1948. Here is their resolution on immigration. Here is their clear, consistent, co-ordinated policy!
A national policy for the development of Canada's natural resources and industrial capacity merits and makes necessary the introduction of a long range immigration policy calculated to bring into Canada selected immigrants whose qualifications are such as to effectively permit them to be assimilated into our democratic way of life.
Let me add that I did not split the infinitive, sir. It continues:
Such immigration should be conducted in close co-operation between the dominion and the provinces.
What is wrong with that?

I did not suggest at any time there was anything wrong with it. In fact, the only words I used were words of

commendation. But when one compares that with the detailed and forthright language used by Mr. Mackenzie King on May 1, 1947, most of which I repeated in a speech I made at Dauphin, Manitoba-and which I would be glad to send to any hon. member who would like to have it, either for reading, or for reference purposes-
Oh, oh.

I am not going to read this speech to the house although, Mr. Speaker,
I am very much tempted to do so. I am proud of it. However, I think I will read the concluding paragraphs because they do attempt to summarize in very general terms what is said in more detail elsewhere in the speech. This was what I said:
There is a mistaken impression in some quarters that the right to migrate from one country to another is one of the rights recognized in the universal declaration of human rights drawn up by the United Nations. It is not.
As the law stands in Canada today and as it has always stood, the only persons who have an unqualified right to be in this country are Canadian citizens and, of course, the Sovereign.
Immigrants who have been in Canada long enough to acquire Canadian domicile, but who have not yet become citizens, have very considerable legal rights and, under the existing law, immigration officers have no right to prevent them from returning to Canada so long as they retain their Canadian domicile.
But parliament has always reserved to the government the right to select the persons who may be admitted to this country as immigrants with the intention of becoming members of our national household.
Parliament has laid down certain principles to govern the selection of immigrants, and the government itself has laid down more detailed regulations based on those principles.
Broadly speaking, these principles boil down to this. We try to select as immigrants those who will have to change their ways least in order to adapt themselves to Canadian life and to contribute to the development of the Canadian nation. That is why entry to Canada is virtually free to citizens of the United Kingdom, the United States and France so long as they have good health and good characters.
Was that all one paragraph?

That is why a deliberate preference is shown for immigrants from countries with political and social institutions similar to our own. That is why a deliberate preference is given to the relatives of Canadian citizens and other persons already resident in Canada. And that is why a deliberate preference is given to people possessing qualifications or occupations which give them an opportunity for employment or establishment.
In all these cases, the immigrant, other things being equal, is likely to find his feet faster and to adapt himself to our ways better than other immigrants without these qualifications.
All this is not to say that we set up, or pretend to set up, immigrants from some countries or of some races as being superior to others in an absolute or intrinsic sense. All we are saying is that we have already built a certain kind of nation here in the northern half of North America and

that we want to preserve the kind of nation we have built and that we want to admit, as partners in the development of our nation, those newcomers we consider are most likely to help us most to maintain and develop the kind of nation we want Canada to remain.

Mr. Speaker, as an endurance marathon the house has indeed had an example this afternoon of the number of words that could be placed side by side in a period of two hours and leave the house without any knowledge whatsoever of the immigration policy of this country. Indeed, as I listened to the hon. member and recalled that at one time he was the custodian of many of the ideas of a former prime minister, I could not help but conclude that I might paraphrase the policy of another day: immigration if necessary, but not necessarily immigration. It was an unusual speech. It brought the house once more back to the days when the ability to draw on classical allusions and quote from forgotten history was common. The house has lost that talent in recent years. The minister revealed his erudition when he recalled the days of Boadicea. I could not but conclude that his ideas of immigration were indeed secured from those days when Boadicea lived in England and did not wish immigrants from Europe to overrun that country.
It was an interesting speech. If ever the words of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) were established by a minister of the crown, they were this afternoon by the minister. He said that a mess was left to the present minister by his predecessor. The minister established beyond any doubt today that the only difference between what he inherited and what now exists is a few more ingredients which he himself has added while he has been in office.
As I listened to the enunciation of the absolutism in that department I realized some of the reasons that the department of immigration and the department of Indian affairs should be joined together in these two "I" departments. The minister gave us to understand that as far as immigration is concerned, and-certainly as far as Indian affairs are concerned, whatever he decides to do is indeed proper and fitting, and ought not to be challenged in the courts of our country.
I said it should be challenged in parliament.

I do not want to quote anyone who is prejudiced. The minister says that the immigration laws of this country are being administered in a way that is equitable, in a manner that recognizes the fact that we are dealing not with digits but
Immigration
with human beings. I quote as the first witness not one who is prejudiced but one of the most distinguished jurists in our country, a man who I believe was the successor of the Prime Minister as one of the senior officials of the Canadian Bar Association, one of the men who represented this country in San Francisco in 1945. I refer to Chief Justice Farris of British Columbia, a man who at one time, while in politics, was a supporter of this government, a man whose brother, one of the most distinguished of the Canadian bar, is a senator of our country. This is what he said on January 19, 1955:
Immigration officials are "fooling the public".
As I listened to my hon. friend I came to the conclusion that that attitude of mind extended to those in the most senior positions in the department of immigration. Chief Justice Farris said:
Department is circumventing the Immigration Act.
The minister says: "Trust me. We will not do anything wrong if we have absolute power. Just trust us; we know." I watched the Prime Minister as my hon. friend revealed his attitude toward the legal profession when he said: We dare not let solicitors know the reason that we refuse admission to immigrants from other lands because they might use the information improperly. Never in my experience in the house has there been a greater calumny levelled against the members of the legal profession. Does my hon. friend not know that even if undesirable individuals find their way into the legal profession, that any information they have secured as solicitors cannot be used? Yet his explanation as to the reason that solicitors should not be made aware in any way of the hidden Star Chamber reasons which deny prospective immigrants the right to come to this country is that he is afraid the lawyers might take advantage of it.
That was the attitude taken in the reign of Charles I by the then head of the Star Chamber when he once said: "We administer justice; we need no lawyers, and whatever we do is right." That was said in 1642, and Your Honour will recall that the person on behalf of whom that statement was made lost a head, and a good one, in consequence of the Star Chamber activities.
I read you another judgment. On November 19, 1954, a recent appointee to the supreme court of Ontario, Mr. Justice Stewart, said, as reported in the Toronto Star:
If immigration department regulations require Czechoslovakia-born Vojen Cech, now in Canada as a visitor, to return to Venezuela to apply for entry into this country as an immigrant, it is utter nonsense.

Immigration
Yesterday in the city of Montreal a former member of this house, Mr. Justice Rheaume, made this statement when George Sylvestre Simmonds, a Jamaican student at the University of Toronto, who married a Canadian girl, was about to be deported and made an application by way of habeas corpus to stay in Canada. There was nothing he could do. He then went on to say this:
The department had failed to establish a justifiable cause for the deportation, but the order had to be complied with because all the legal formalities had been followed.
That was yesterday. The judge said that there was no justification for sending this Jamaican home. He was a good citizen. The judge then uttered these words which my hon. friend might engrave on the doorway into his office:
"I cannot remain indifferent to sentiments of hospitality"-
Yes, the letter of the law killeth. My hon. friend says, trust us. He places himself on a pedestal and says that the decisions that he in his omnipotence makes shall be unchallenged. That statement was made by him today. I do not say that mistakes will not be made. My hon. friend points out that several hundred thousand people have come into Canada since 1945.
Over a million.

Over a million, yes, but two come in and one goes out. Over a million. Yes, mistakes will be made. There is bound to be some bungling and there are bound to be injustices in individual cases. I would not hold a minister of the government responsible for those things because they happen so long as men are subject to the ordinary vicissitudes and emotions of life.
In so far as the administration of this department is concerned, this is the first time that I know, when bungling has become the cornerstone of policy, when what is done by the supreme authority of this department is to be placed above the courts of our land. One judge after another has had to conclude that, indeed, if the department uses a reasonable degree of care, however tyrannical the decision may be, that decision is not challengeable in the courts. That is why this motion was brought before parliament.
My hon. friend says that we did not raise this motion last year. The reason it was not raised from time to time when we went into supply was that we did not expect that what had been done in 1935, and in 1952, putting off immigration to the last, had become a way of action to be continued in 1954.
What is being done today in the immigration department has been described by the

Edmonton Journal as a national scandal. It refers to the arbitrary and secretive manner in which cases are handled, to say nothing of the outright favouritism displayed on some occasions. When there is no recourse to the courts the power of discrimination becomes intensified. Delays have been inexcusable. I have case after case here of people being pushed around, of arrogance and abuse of authority. These are the things that the courts of this country have objected to.
This afternoon we welcomed the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to this house. In June, 1954, during the last days of the session he asked for a royal commission to investigate what has been recognized by papers across our country, without regard to party, as a mess. He repeated that request in September when he returned from abroad. The need for it was proved today by the minister in his speech. In the presence of my leader I say that what has taken place can no longer be permitted to continue without intensive examination through a royal commission, to the end that the actions of the last year, the last two years and the last three years shall not become a continued and perpetual portion of the administration of that department.
My hon. friend has said to the hon. member for Kamloops "What has Magna Carta to do with it?" I was surprised to hear that statement from my hon. friend with his vast erudition in history. What has Magna Carta to do with it? Long years ago in 1215 Magna Carta made a declaration, and it has been of the essence of the British peoples ever since: to no man will we deny, to no man will we delay, justice.
Is there anyone in this house who will tell me that when the minister is despotic and highhanded, when he rides roughshod over the statute, when he substitutes the caprice of a minister for the will of parliament, the courts of this country should not have the right to say: You shall not do that. My hon. friend says that the courts do not understand, and I am going to refer to that a little later because that is the attitude of the departmental senior official. The minister says: You have an appeal! An appeal to Caesar, to the minister himself. An appeal from the hired man to the hired man's boss.
What a travesty on justice it is that a minister under the power granted by parliament makes regulations, the officials interpret the regulations on a day-to-day basis without uniformity, they decide the rights of the individual in secret and refuse to let the individual know their reasons for making a decision. I thought that all this had been swept aside generations ago. When the department lost a case in the courts what did

it do? It delayed doing anything. The minister says that when a decision is made the individual has a recourse, but that recourse is in mandamus, which places upon him the onus to establish a right which the minister denies exists in the individual.
There have been postponements and infinite delays. People desirous of coming to our country have waited, and the answer given is that they cannot come yet, that they may be able to come some time in the future. Hope may spring eternal in the human breast but that does not apply to those who have made application to come to Canada under our present immigration laws.
Does the house know what the deputy minister said with regard to appeals to the courts? Winnipeg is a place known to both the minister and me. We both know the Fort Garry hotel in Winnipeg. It was in Winnipeg, but not in the Fort Garry hotel, that the Canadian Bar Association had its meeting. I am not saying anything against Colonel Fortier because he is merely carrying out the regulations of two ministers, but he did give an answer there.
Somebody suggested that the individual should be given recourse to the courts. My hon. friend will agree that to deny to the individual the right of his day in court invariably builds up power in those who are above challenge, and permits them to treat the rights of the individual as nonexistent. At the meeting of the Canadian Bar Association in Winnipeg, the following resolution was passed regarding these powers:
1.	Due notice of the proceedings before any board to any person directly concerned therein.
2.	Notice of the facts which the administrative body considers relevant to the complaint or proceeding.
3.	The right to anyone adversely affected thereby to contest the allegations which would include in appropriate cases the right to cross-examine.
4.	The right to have counsel before administrative agencies.
5.	An obligation upon administrative tribunals to set forth the facts which they find and the reasons for their decision.
That was the resolution of the law society of Ontario of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is a member.
What did the deputy minister say when it was suggested that the individual should have a right of recourse to the courts? This is what he said:
One danger in giving the rejected applicant recourse to the courts is that a court may reach a final decision. The beauty of the department's present system is that the civil service can review and review and review and the applicant always has the hope that some day he may be admitted.
That is a masterpiece of an explanation against having cases taken to the court, namely because about cases in the courts
Immigration
there is a finality that does not exist in these administrative bodies and that as to those people who want to come, although they have been turned down, the cases may be reviewed and some day, somewhere, the individuals may be admitted to Canada. Then he also said this:
Sometimes the department might make a slip and deal with a lawyer's client. If we allowed applicants to know why they were rejected it would be a wrong thing for the protection of the country.
Somebody asked Mr. Fortier this question: Why would it be wrong to tell the individual why he was turned down? And he gave in effect the same answer that the minister gave today: "I am afraid I cannot say why". Mr. Speaker, this is the institution that my hon. friend defends today. I hold no brief for any member of the committee on civil liberties that dealt with the subject of immigration. That committee was composed of three lawyers: Mr. McDonald who is even at the present time, according to his recent statement, head of the Liberal organization in this part of Ontario; Mr. Dickey-and I use that form because his name appears here in that way-the senior member for Halifax, for whom I have the highest regard; and Mr. Taylor, with whom I am unacquainted. This committee was set up for the purpose of investigating the situation that existed in the department of immigration. The committee met. They had a series of meetings and I intend to refer to them if I have time to do so. They made certain recommendations. My hon. friend read those recommendations and I am not going to repeat them. Then apparently things started to move.
I was greatly surprised at my hon. friend today speaking in such disparaging terms of Mr. McDonald. He gave us to understand that Mr. McDonald was a man who would make a spectacularly unjustifiable speech in order to attain prominence in the press. My hon. friend is in a position to judge him; I am not. But that was his considered opinion.
Those were not exactly my words.
Oh, no. I have understated it, as my hon. friend said. I understated my hon. friend's words.
I said he was a Liberal politician.

As a matter of fact, my hon. friend told us that he was a student of words and of the dictionary, having been trained under Mr. King to get the finest shades of meaning of words as they appeared in the dictionary.

Immigration
That is why he said what he said this afternoon.

Here is what Mr. McDonald said. Mr. McDonald came back to Ottawa.
Still "stunned" by the "surprising" reaction to the report, Mr. McDonald returned to Ottawa only today to find himself accused in some quarters of "political treachery".
Possibly my hon. friend would be able to fill in the facts about the person who held such a view of Mr. McDonald's public activities.
For two years the bar association subcommittee on civil liberties, of which Mr. McDonald was chairman, had been investigating the operations of the immigration department.
Then he goes on to say this. He says he held a press conference. Then he really opened up. He told what he knew of the department. In speaking of him, my hon. friend was rather disparaging when he spoke over the radio on a press conference. He said that Mr. McDonald did not have much experience in immigration, except as a lawyer. Anyway, Mr. McDonald said that he stood behind everything he had said not only in the report in which he was joined by the senior member for Halifax but also in the press conference and the various statements made by him. In other words, the stand that Mr. McDonald took was this: "I am unrepentant and what I said is unrevised but true". Mr. Dickey, the senior member for Halifax, resigned from the committee. The minister explained that he did so but he went on to say-and I say this with the greatest respect for the senior member for Halifax-that while Mr. Dickey had resigned as a member of the committee, he had not refuted the statements contained in the report.
What was the report? That report has been placed before you, Mr. Speaker. It was a report in which was revealed the fact that a committee on civil liberties had brought matters to the attention of the then minister, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), on several occasions. My hon. friend referred to the report attached to the report given by this committee and it states as follows:
Four meetings of the full committee were held In Ottawa-
That means that all three members were present.
-and eight other meetings of two members of the committee were held in Ottawa and Montreal.
It goes on to say that they brought these things to the attention of the minister:
In its 1953 report, the committee recommended certain administrative reforms within the Department of Citizenship and Immigration itself and the creation of an immigration appeal board based on a judicial and legal concept.

Surely that was a reasonable request. These lawyers were endeavouring to bring about a removal of the tyrannical conduct of the department. They did not regard political considerations as of any importance. They rose above that consideration. I ask you, could you have a more impartial jury to look into the activities of the immigration department than Mr. McDonald and the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey)? Incidentally, Mr. McDonald says he is going to run next time in Carleton constituency. There is a question mark at the end of that statement in the report, but I think that was an error. This was the report which they forwarded in 1954. They asked for possible codification of regulations issued by the department and the publication of interdepartmental directives to field officers. They did that to the end that there would be uniformity so that there would be no discrimination for or against anyone in the making of decisions, and so that there would be an approach to unity among the various officials.
They asked for the implementation of proper and legal appeal procedures as recommended in last year's report of the subcommittee. They asked for the establishment of a procedure setting forth reasons for rejections in each case in such a way as to give the rejected party or the applicant concerned an opportunity of overcoming the department's objections. Finally, they asked that the committee's recommendations made in the 1953 report be implemented. In their report the three members of the subcommittee said:
Your subcommittee expresses regret that no action has been taken by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to implement any of the recommendations contained in its 1953 report. We recommend that the subcommittee be continued for a further year, that it be instructed to continue to examine the administration of immigration laws and- regulations in accordance with its terms of reference . . .
Now, sir, why were these recommendations not accepted? My hon. friend brushed them aside and said that there was not much in them. I have read the material part but there are some other very interesting parts dealing with why reasons should be given. The report says:
Few Canadians realize that the minister need not: (a) notify his own department as to why he adopted a certain course . . .

If the immigration service can proceed in this way it is a travesty on justice and a serious danger to the success of administrative procedures, and secondly, if judicial procedures are defeated by administrative procedures by the department .	.	. then liberties are being whittled away
from all.
It is submitted that it is unthinkable that parliament ever intended that the minister could deport persons or admit persons, and remain silent as to why he took such action because of some "personal matter".

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why my hon. friend did not choose people he could rely upon to be members of the committee. After all, his name is there, and there is an old proverb that what is written down even a team of horses cannot pull out. Yes, that is the record, and it is a record that indicates that these gentlemen did in fact bring up a matter of singular importance, one that deserved attention, in 1953 and in 1954. But the law still remains unchanged and the uncontrolled despotism of unknown bureaucrats sitting in a Star Chamber is still a part of the law so far as immigration is concerned.
My time is almost up, but I should like to point out that evidence as to the operation of the immigration regulations is to be found in the files of almost every member of the house. It is to be found in the judgments of superior courts. It is to be found also in the record to which I have just made reference. I am not going into these examples which I have. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) over the years has stated, and I do not contradict him in any way, that in every case he read over these files. However admirable my hon. friend may be, and I would be the last to say anything to the contrary, to place him in a position where in his unchallengeable power, in the secrecy of his own office, he can determine my rights is something that shocks the sensibilities of those who believe that the courts of the land are standing guard over the rights of the people.
I shall give one example that came to hand the other day. A number of Canadians left here in 1947 for Yugoslavia, no doubt attracted by the specious promises of communism. Then, they tried to come back. There is a record here of one Canadian whose family came back, but who has been denied the right to return. He asks: What business have you to say to me, as a Canadian, that I cannot return to my own land? Canada did take its part in the United Nations in support of the principle of the right of a citizen to return to his own land. For several years this man has been trying to return. He asks, "Why can I not come? I will not be a public charge." The answer, in effect, is that this department knows best.

The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) set out our views in that admirable and masterly address that opened this debate the other day. All I have tried to do was to fill in some of the needs for alteration of the laws of this country to make the department of immigration a department of immigration rather than a department that places in the hands of a minister the power to say when the tap shall be on or the tap shall be off, and that whatever he decides is final, for he is above the courts.
If the courts decide against him, then he may try the old route of order in council to circumvent the courts, or he may delay carrying out the orders of the courts thereby, in effect saying to the courts of the land, "You may declare, but we can postpone." This party asks for a royal commission to investigate this whole business, and to investigate what the press of our country almost without exception regards as deliberate confusion.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, in my experience before the courts I have been very much interested to follow the trials presided over by Chief Justice Sir Frangois Lemieux. He was a great criminal lawyer, a man of great experience and was acknowledged by all as one of the most able jurists of his time. One day there came before him the case of a fellow who had stolen some property from somewhere in the district. His counsel spoke along the same lines as did the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and referred to Magna Carta, and also to the king who had died in a tragic manner. He referred to King Charles, to Louis XVI and Emperor Nicholas of Russia, as well as to others. He said, "This is why tyrants have died."
When the judge came to deliver his address to the jury he said, "One has spoken about Emperor Nicholas of Russia, about King Louis XVI of France and King Charles of England. But forget all that, and think of the defendant"-so and so, of such and such a place-"who has stolen property and is now before the court facing that accusation." The judge said that to the jury, and the jury gave to the judge's statement the weight it deserved.
As my hon. friend has spoken about the past and the dead, I shall answer his quotation from the great beyond by another quotation from the great beyond, and refer to a statement that was made in the presence of the hon. member, right here in the House of Commons, in May of 1947 by the then leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Mackenzie King. He enunciated a realistic Canadian immigration policy in which he stressed four points-and I want my hon. friend to listen to them, because it is the basis of my argument this evening:
First, to increase the population by permanent and carefully selected immigrants;
Second, not to exceed the capacity of absorption of our national economy;
Third, not to bring any fundamental change in the ethnical character of the population.
Those were matters that were overlooked by the hon. member and by other speakers
Immigration
from the other side of the house-unless they agreed with them. Then:
Fourth-and this is the main point to which I wish to bring the attention of the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton)-the access into Canada is not a human right. It is a privilege that the Canadian nation alone can grant. It is a matter of domestic policy.
Well, you cannot use mandamus to force the minister to give an applicant something that is not his right. The applicant must first have the right to it; and nobody outside Canada has the right to insist upon coming here. He must be here only if the government of the country accepts him as a Canadian. If not, he must stay out. And it is as the minister has said, that the applications made were much more numerous than those that were granted. Or, according to the words of the Scripture: Many are called but few are chosen.
The hon. member has spoken only in generalities-that is, with the exception of two cases, when he mentioned the Simmonds case and the Prpich case. The newspaper article I read said that the judge had declared that it was an unprecedented case- which means that there was no precedent for it. I hope my hon. friend follows me when I say that "unprecedented" means that there was no precedent beforehand. Is that clear, now? It means that it was the first time it had happened.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member means that it had never happened before.

I presume that it means that it never happened before. It is the one and only case of that kind. And my hon. friend knows no more about it than I do, because probably we both read it from the same paper. It shows that the judge was very friendly. He made a recommendation to the department which had never been made before.
My hon. friend curses the department, but makes no useful recommendation, except the one of a royal commission, just as if members of parliament were non-entities and unable to look after their business. It is the same story: Abandonment of parliamentary responsibility.
Then he quoted two sentences from one judge, Chief Justice Farris, for whom I have great respect:
The department is circumventing the Immigration Act. Immigration officials are fooling the public.
This is what was said by the chief justice of British Columbia. I know him by sight

Immigration
only, never having had the privilege of meeting him. But he gives no facts-just the same as the members of the opposition-no facts; just generalities.
And the other judge, Mr. Justice Stewart, said:
If the immigration department regulations prevent a Czechoslovakian to return to Venezuela, it is nonsense.
That is one other case, the opinion of another judge. If my hon. friend suggests a royal commission, then he will insist upon judges being appointed thereon. If such a royal commission were appointed, I would challenge the right of Chief Justice Farris and of Mr. Justice Stewart to sit on it, because of prejudice.
Now, here is the report of the bar association subcommittee on civil liberties. The gentlemen who sat on it are persons for whom I have great respect, but evidently they were not familiar with the views of my old leader, as he expressed them.
And now, immediately after that reference to the subcommittee of the bar association on civil liberties, I shall read again the fourth pronouncement of Mr. King about a realistic policy on immigration:
The access into Canada is not a human right; it is a privilege that the Canadian nation alone can grant. It is a matter of domestic policy.
This is what the hon. member for Prince Albert does not understand, although he argued, as well as anyone could do it, the case of the rejected applicants who desire to migrate here. But then, speaking always as if the immigrants had the right to force the minister to grant their application to come to Canada, he cited the arbitrary and secretive manner in which cases are handled. The minister has to render account to parliament. He spoke more modestly than the hon. member for Prince Albert ever did. He admitted that sometimes he could make mistakes. Then the hon. gentleman spoke of the outright favouritism displayed on some occasions.
Who defended the minister this afternoon? The hon. member for Prince Albert himself, because I took notes and here is what he said, if I took down his words correctly:
However tyrannical the decision may be it is not challengeable in the courts. That is why the motion was brought before parliament.
We will not have to go to the show any more.

No, I am so glad. I share the applause for the hon. member for Prince Albert and I admit that he is by far my superior in eloquence. I want to be as modest

as the minister, and it is just as well to be humble. Politics is a great lesson in modesty and humility.

Conservatives.

There is bound to be some bungling and there are bound to be injustices in individual cases. I would not hold a minister-
Mark you, sir, listen, Mr. Speaker; this is the hon. member for Prince Albert speaking:

The minister is the hon. gentleman who is the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration of the St. Laurent government.
