This is the first time in my whole long parliamentary career that a cabinet minister has been at the same time attacked and defended by the same member of parliament in the same speech. One must be an artist to realize such stunts. Then, there was the Prpich case. The hon. member mentioned it in a strange manner. I took some notes. The hon. member said:
I shall give one example that came to hand the other day. A number of Canadians left here in 1947 for Yugoslavia, no doubt attracted by the specious promises of communism. Then, they tried to come back. There is a record here of one Canadian whose family came back, but who has been denied the right to return. He asks: What business have you to say to me, as a Canadian, that I cannot return to my own land? Canada did take its part in the United Nations in support of the principle of the right of a citizen to return to his own land.
' I agree with my hon. friend; a Canadian may have the right to come here unless he has got into difficulty of some kind elsewhere. Then he would be subject to the punishment of the courts. But if he is a Canadian he is subject to the laws of justice in this country. However, I do not know anything about that case. It may be as bad as my hon. friend says. The hon. gentleman mentioned two cases, the Simmonds case and the Prpich case. All the rest were generalities. I am sorry, because my hon. friend is so gifted. There is a Latin phrase which goes as follows: "Nascuntur poetae, fiunt oratores". One is

born a poet; one becomes an orator. My hon. friend was born an orator. He has all the gifts, and I regret that he did not treat the important subject of immigration as it deserved to be treated. Instead of attacking and defending the minister at the same time, he should have replied to the hon. member for Kamloops. It was up to him, with his experience, to establish before this parliament and the country that the hon. member for Kamloops spoke through his hat, and it would have been a wonderful experience.
I now come to it, if the house will listen to me. It will not be long. I will take the second ground of complaint of the hon. member for Kamloops. He said, as reported at page 1163 of Hansard:
The second branch of our criticism of the government under this heading, that immigration policies are not in conformity with the needs and responsibilities of Canada, is the concern we feel because the government has neglected British immigration.
And on the following page:
Our criticism of the government here is based on the fact that by their negligence and inattention, they are losing for Canada one of the most desirable sources of immigrants.
And then, in conclusion:
These facts, Mr. Speaker, support our contention that the government is not paying sufficient regard to immigration and the potentialities of immigration from the United Kingdom.
Now, I will deliver the speech that the hon. member for Prince Albert should have delivered in answer to the hon. member for Kamloops.
What was that again?

My hon. friend arrives just in time. I was just about to deliver the speech that the hon. member for Prince Albert should have delivered to confound the hon. member for Kamloops. I say that in all modesty and humility because it is not my speech; it is the speech of the hon. member for Prince Albert. It is about immigration to and from the United Kingdom and the commonwealth of British nations. A total of 6,900 people left Canada to go to the United Kingdom, while
44,000	Britishers came to Canada. A total of 11,500 left Australia to go to the United Kingdom while 30,600 went from the United Kingdom to Australia. Those who left New Zealand for the United Kingdom totalled 3,400 as opposed to 14,600 who left the United Kingdom for New Zealand. A total of 4,300 left South Africa for the United Kingdom and 6,600 left the United Kingdom for South Africa. Figures are given for other parts of the empire.
The total of those who left commonwealth countries to go to the United Kingdom was
Immigration
62,100 while the total of those who left the United Kingdom to go to Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Southern Rhodesia, East and West Africa, India, Pakistan and other countries of the commonwealth was 127,800. That indicates that the number leaving the United Kingdom for various parts of the commonwealth was a little more than twice as much as the number of those who left commonwealth countries to go to Great Britain.
The migration from the British Isles to commonwealth countries totalled 127,800. Those who left the United Kingdom not including Ireland for the United States totalled 65,361, whereas those who left Eire for the United States totalled 17,756. The total number of migrants from the British Isles to commonwealth countries and the United States was 210,917. A total of 4,900 Britishers came to Canada via the United States, making a total of 53,492 British immigrants coming to Canada, or nearly one-half the total of British migration to commonwealth countries; one-quarter of the total migration to the United States, and more than two-fifths of British migration to commonwealth countries. That is something.
What should be stressed at the present is that we should respect the desires of the immigrant. I am not precisely an academic advocate of a bill of rights or other frills of that kind, but I believe that we should respect the liberty and freedom of those who want to migrate from one country to another. This is a principle of freedom which cannot be denied by anyone.
Those who migrated from the British Isles were absolutely free to make their choice as to whether they would go to any part of the commonwealth or to the United States. They made that choice and no one can challenge their right. The total immigration into Canada was 144,692. British immigration including those who come through the United States amounted to 53,000. The total immigration into Australia in 1953, the last figure we have, was 163,125; British immigration amounted to 30,600, about one-fifth. Immigration into New Zealand amounted to 62,712 with British immigration totalling 14,600.
My hon. friend should have said that immigrants, British or otherwise, are perfectly free to make a choice as to country. No one can prevent them from doing that. I could have understood my hon. friend making a charge against the department if he had said that so many Britishers who wanted to come to Canada had been denied access to this country. He said nothing of the sort; he spoke of two or three cases out of a total of 174,000.

Immigration
I suggest that my hon. friend read the report of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. It is a most valuable document, more important than Hansard. It is more important than the opinions of two or three judges or of a subcommittee of the bar association. It contains facts which he should know.
I referred to the 174,000 immigrants that came here last year. Of that number, only 2,213 were refused admission. When I saw that figure I thought the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would come here with an arraignment of the minister, with instances of those who had suffered injustice. Nothing of the sort, and there were 2,213 who had been refused admission.
They were communists.

They are indicated as being mental and medical cases so probably they were communists. My hon. friend does not deny anything about that. The deportations numbered 630. That is a fine canvas for a long space. My hon. friend did not say anything about it. Where he missed the boat was when he did not speak of the qualifications of the immigrants and the necessity of their accepting our mode of life and becoming Canadian citizens, as most of them have.
It is most important in the first place to make the right selection. I suggest to the minister that he get in touch with the Department of External Affairs in order that there is no mistake in making the right selections. In the second place there is the question of absorption and the accepting of the incoming people as good Canadians. This is a very important thing and a long speech could be made about it. They should be taught patriotism. They should be told that they have a fine future here provided that they work. They should be told that they cannot rely on the social legislation when they come here. They must help themselves, be good Canadians, and work just as the majority of Canadian people do. They should be told that at the start. Then they would not be deceived. Some of them come here to get allowances and benefits of every description. They must be told that Canada is the finest country in the world, that it will become their country by adoption, and that they will become true Canadians but that they must be worthy of this country and must give evidence of their worthiness by contributing to the general welfare of all.
I do not intend to speak any longer, Mr. Speaker. I could make a much longer speech; I could speak twice as long as did the minister this afternoon, but I would not have the opportunity to do so. I would be stopped.

However, I must tell the hon. gentleman that he is greatly mistaken if he thinks that the Conservative party will get a vote from the speeches that have been made by the Conservative party on the immigration policies of the government. The Canadian people are no fools. They will realize that there is nothing in them and they will say "Poor Kamloops" and "Poor Prince Albert".

Mr. Speaker, I feel rather like someone who has strayed by mistake onto the stage where on the same bill we have Sir Laurence Olivier and Fridolin. I am sure I cannot compete with either of them. I have no rodomontade and no drollery to offer you. In fact, I am not at all sure that this is actually a subject that either of those methods suits. On the other hand, I have some rather hard, grim, indigestible facts for the minister to try his teeth on.
I should say first that I do not hold the opinion of the minister that is held by some hon. members who spoke this afternoon. I do not think he is a Caesar; I do not think he has that vaulting ambition. I do not think he has the sinister character that has been painted. Admittedly I have a soft spot in my heart for him as one must have for someone who once loaned him a pair of pants to save him from sartorial disaster. In addition to that, I always have a weakness for intelligence wherever I find it, even in such an unlikely place as the treasury benches. But I am afraid that the minister, like some of his predecessors, has become a prisoner of some rather dubious elements in the public administration.
I was interested yesterday during the speech of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) when the minister asked him if he had the judgment on the Leong Ba Chai case and the hon. member for Kamloops said no, that he did not have it. Then today the minister quoted from that judgment, and I presume he had it in his hand; but curiously enough he was not able to answer my question when I asked him if the supreme court and the appeal court of British Columbia had not given precisely the same judgment. He said he did not know. He was not able to answer me. Yet curiously enough, in the judgment of Mr. Justice Taschereau, we read this:
Mr. Justice Clyne, before whom the application was made, directed the issue of a writ of mandamus ordering the immigration officer forthwith to consider the said application, and the court of appeal of British Columbia unanimously confirmed this decree.
We have this curious situation. We have this infallible department that is not content with the supreme court of British Columbia

telling them that they are wrong, telling them that they are wrong on a point of law, and that they do not know the law; not content with that, they have to appeal to the court of appeal of British Columbia and the court of appeal of British Columbia tells them precisely the same thing. Then what do they do? They bring the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada, at heaven only knows what cost to the taxpayers of Canada.
I would not lay so much stress on this matter, Mr. Speaker, but for the fact that, on looking back through many of the judgments,
I find that this is apparently the usual course of procedure of this infallible department. It is never satisfied with one judgment against it. It must line up two or three other judgments and finally get kicked in the teeth here in Ottawa by the Supreme Court of Canada.
On this particular case it is quite true- as the minister told us this afternoon-that after the finding of the Supreme Court of Canada the department at long last obeyed the instructions of the court and entertained the application of Leong Ba Chai from Hong Kong. Admittedly it was probably a long process because he was in Hong Kong. But the original application took place in 1952. Not a single thing has been changed since that time. They had a decision of a competent supreme court in British Columbia. Had they at that time obeyed the instructions of the supreme court of British Columbia, this young man might have reached Canada before his father died. It is a rather pathetic footnote to this squalid tale of stupidity, arrogance and incompetence that this old man finally died before his son was able to enter Canada.
It is not only cases of this kind that the infallible department of immigration drags through court after court; it is also the procedure with cases of people who are going to be deported. It may be perfectly true- as the minister has been at great pains to tell us again and again-that these applicants for immigration have no rights whatever, but that they merely have privileges that we grant. However, it is a different proposition in the case of someone who is resident in Canada and whose case is suddenly pulled out of the files by the immigration department, as was the case of a lady in Toronto recently. I refer to a lady by the name of Brent, an American lady who married a Canadian and who came legally into this country.
Does the minister wish to ask a question?

I was wondering whether that case was not still before the courts and whether the hon. gentleman felt he ought to discuss it while it was before the courts. I have no objection-
Immigration

That is fine. It is before the courts. I am glad the minister told me that. I thought probably that was the case, that it might again be dragged to the third court. Of course I will not discuss it. Instead of doing that, I will discuss a case which has been disposed of by the courts and which is entirely on all fours with the Brent case. In fact, the judgments are on the same point. I want to read to the house and to the minister a rather scathing indictment of the department's behaviour which apparently is the same as it was in 1932 when this judgment was given by the late* Sir Lyman Duff.
This was the case of a Japanese, and curiously enough it was a Japanese who was picked up on the street in Nanaimo.
Did the hon. member say that was in 1932?
He surely does not expect us to take responsibility for what was done in 1932.

No; I am not
expecting you to do that but I am expecting you to take responsibility for your stupidity and incompetence in 1955; you are pursuing precisely the same policy for which the supreme court rapped the department in 1932. That is the point. You have not learned anything. This young Japanese came to Canada perfectly legally. His uncle was his sponsor. He came to Nanaimo. He set up a restaurant. This young man was going to be a cook in the restaurant. Shortly after he arrived the uncle fell sick and had to close his restaurant and this young man had to find other employment, as he did; but he was picked up in the other employment by officials of the department of immigration and they were going to deport him. They refused to divulge to him the reasons for which he was being deported, just as they had refused to divulge the reasons in the case which I must not discuss in 1955.
Sir Lyman Duff had this to say:
The chief question I desire to discuss is the effect of section 23 of the Immigration Act. The words, "had, made or given under the authority and in accordance with the provisions of this act relating to the detention or deportation of any rejected immigrant, passenger or other person, upon any ground whatsoever, unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile", are an essential part of this section; and its disqualifying provisions obviously can only take effect where the conditions expressed in these words are fulfilled.
In particular, the phrase "in accordance with the provisions of this act" cannot be neglected; their meaning is plain. The "order" returned as
The word "late" teas incorrectly used-see page 1279.

Immigration
justifying the detention must be "in accordance with the provisions of this act." It must not. that is to say, be essentially an order made in disregard of some substantive condition laid down by the act. This applies to the order of the minister as well as to the order of the board of inquiry.
The order of the minister must be an order directing the investigation of facts alleged in a complaint made to him; and such facts, unless the enactment is to be reduced to the merest parade of words, must be alleged, of course, in such a manner as to make the allegation reasonably intelligible to the person against whom the investigation is directed.
The jurisdiction of the board, as an investigating body, is limited to the investigation of the facts alleged, a condition, again, implying intelligibility of allegation. Indeed, unless the person concerned is to have a reasonable opportunity of knowing the nature of the allegations, what is the purpose of requiring his presence?
Now, Mr. Speaker, the point of all this is that this particular judgment was quoted in the courts in connection with the Brent case which the minister now tells us he is going to drag to the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not know how many times they have to be dragged through the courts at public expense before these infallible people will accept the fact that certain things must be complied with if the law is to be carried out.
I come to another case, and this one has some rather interesting features too. This is a case in 1952 before the courts of Ontario where again the department of immigration decided that they had grounds for deporting a man who came from the West Indies. His name was Legge, and it was alleged that he was a rather unsuitable person to be a citizen of Canada, which he may have been. I do not know. But the point is that he was in this country for a considerable period before there was any attempt made to deport him and it was not-and this is very important-until his wife and children arrived from the West Indies and proved to be of a different hue from the minister of citizenship and immigration and myself that they decided he was an unsuitable person to be a resident of Canada.

speechtext: On a question of privilege, the question of the hue had nothing to do with the case. The file was opened and shown to the leader of the party to which my hon. friend belongs.

I know it was opened and, moreover, I know that the minister had had complaints about this man upon which he had not acted until these other circumstances arose. Moreover, in that file there is not a single statement of conviction for the criminal record he is alleged to have had in Jamaica. Has the minister got anything to say to that? Can he produce that evidence of conviction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There were no evidences of conviction. There were letters and documents indicating convictions. I have forgotten the first point my hon. friend made. What else did my hon. friend say?

That you had no
evidence of conviction and that you had had representations in this case for some considerable time before action was taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not recall that. This gentleman got into difficulties in the town of Col-lingwood and, as I recall, moved to London. During that time people were complaining about him and when we found where he was we took action.
On what grounds was he deported, and was he given the facts of the case against him? Did he have an opportunity to refute the arguments of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: At the moment I cannot say to what extent he was given that, but I know that at the time of the hearing he was well aware of all charges against him. How much earlier than the hearing I must say I cannot say now.
At the time of the hearing he saw all the charges against him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Next case.

There was no evidence of conviction and the minister to this day has not got in his files any substantive evidence of a criminal record for this man. I can only say that it is a most remarkable coincidence that when this man's family arrived from the West Indies it was discovered that he really was an unsuitable resident of Canada. We hear a lot about the famous McCarran Act in the United States, but I am told by lawyers who have appeared before the board of immigration appeals there that they have a very different system from the kangaroo courts that we establish here. I am told that they have a board of immigration appeals upon which no official of the immigration department sits, but legally trained personnel are present and any lawyer, whether he be American or foreign, can appear with full rights before that board.
I am told that all the charges against a person who is to be deported are presented to him and as much time as he wishes can be spent on the case.
I suggest that if we had something of this sort in Canada we would not have these hole-and-corner deportation orders that are taking place after being dragged through court after

court after court. It is all very well for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to tell us as he did this afternoon of the very few deportation orders that have been signed in proportion to the number of immigrants. He did not tell us, however, how many people are warned that if they do not leave the country in a voluntary manner they will be deported. How many are there? I suggest the case would be very different.
I want to appeal to the minister not to take refuge in this silly attitude that there is nothing wrong with his department, because I suggest with all respect that the opinions of the justices of the courts of Canada surely should be treated with at least as much respect as the opinions of the subordinates of the department of immigration, and they do not appear to have been. In fact, it seems to have been the considered policy of the department to ignore every judgment and to go on to get another one, presumably on the advice of departmental officials.
I think there is also this to be considered. It is all very well to say that these people have no rights, but they appear before officials whom you and I do not know. At least, I do not, and I will bet that most of the members of the house do not. We do not know what sort of people they are. We suspect what they are from some of their actions, but to these unfortunates who appear before them they are Canada and they come before these officials with files which may or may not be open. I challenge either the present minister or the former minister to tell the house that in every case, or even in a substantial number of cases, are the files with the charges upon which the deportation order is based made clear to those who are being deported.
Yet again and again the courts of the country have told successive ministers and successive administrators in the department that it is a breach of the law to proceed with deportation unless the unfortunate deportee has had an intelligible statement of the case against him. Again and again, the department has refused to comply with that law. Then they tell us there is nothing wrong in the department. What nonsense! I would very strongly advise the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to take a leaf out of the book of his colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who took very drastic and severe action to clear up the mess in his department, and I gather with salutary results. Certainly, we can all commend the results. I would commend to the minister similar treatment of the interior of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Immigration
So much, sir, for the question of the administration of the present act. There is, I think, something else that perhaps we should consider, and that is the broad picture of immigration into this country. Everyone here has given lip service to the necessity of opening the doors to as many of the best possible people as we can absorb. I am going to go a little bit farther than our friends of the Conservative party went the other day, and suggest that much more strenuous efforts should be made to attract a much larger proportion of people from the British Isles than we have been getting. Before the minister tells me he would be glad to do that, I want to assure him I have some ideas on how it can be done.
I want to point this out. We have heard tonight from what I believe was described as one of the great voices from beyond, enunciating government policy. Apparently no member of this government is able to enunciate policy. They have to call a seance to get policy enunciated. In any event, the ghost has told us several times what the immigration policy for Canada is. I remember there was another statement on immigration policy to the effect that it was the aim of this great and good government to maintain as well as possible the existing ethnic balance in our population. The minister shakes his head. I stand corrected if that is not an accurate statement, but I have heard it several times.

It was the fundamental character of the population. I do not think there was ever anything said about the existing ethnic balance, certainly not in anything I have ever seen that Mr. Mackenzie King said.
Bless my soul, I am not psychic; I do not know what Mr. Mackenzie King said. I have to rely on the statements of living ministers.
Mine is from Hansard.

I should like the minister to tell me just what kind of character he is looking for. Have we a yardstick of nobility that we apply to applicants for immigration? I suggest that is a ridiculous attempt to argue away a plain statement which indicated to the people of Canada roughly what the purpose of the government was, and it was a purpose that was endorsed by the people of Canada. The minister himself said earlier today that we had built a certain type of society here in Canada, and it is believed that the effects of the proportion of our population are such and such between the different ethnic groups, and if we are going to maintain it, as the minister

Immigration
suggested this afternoon he wants to do, then we have to take into consideration the ethnic make-up of our population.
Unfortunately last year, the minister's report tells us, less than one-third of the immigrants came from the British Isles. I am not for a moment decrying the worth of the immigrants who came from the other countries. All I am pointing out is this. Those immigrants come here with very great handicaps, the handicap of a strange land. The immigrants from Great Britain come here with the tremendous advantage of a similarity of language, customs and outlook, so that they can be absorbed much more easily.
There is another aspect to this problem. I do not think anyone would be likely to accuse me of being an imperialist, but I do feel we have a certain responsibility to the people of the British Isles because we have sheltered ourselves behind them on two occasions. We have a certain responsibility for them. They are now facing a serious crisis with regard to population, no matter how their public men speak. They have said it is not a crisis, but they know it is a crisis. All of them know they have a population they cannot hope to support adequately in the future. I believe it is our task in this country to make it as easy as possible for them, not merely through the administration of the department, but as easy as possible owing to economic circumstances. These people would come here with their skills, their inherited outlook on life and a common language with ourselves.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that our ability to absorb new immigrants is closely circumscribed by the level of our investment program. We can have all the orders we like and have the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration going to Britain shedding sweetness and light wherever he goes, but that will not bring another immigrant if there are not economic opportunities waiting here. In that regard we in Canada are faced with a rather depressing picture. In 1954 we had new capital outlays of some $5-8 billion. Business Week, which I do not think anyone would accuse of being a communist document, conducted a survey amongst business people, academic economists and government officials recently to get a consensus of their estimates of the likely capital investment in 1955. Their consensus was that the capital expenditure is expected to drop to $5'75 billion, a slight drop over last year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we are to absorb population, if indeed we are to maintain the present population, we have to have an expanding program of investment. Instead of

that, we are faced with a contracting one. One of the reasons, of course, that our program of capital investment is contracting is the nature of many of the investments that are being made. My colleague the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) mentioned the other day the change in the nature of United States investments in Canada within the last year or so. There has been a change to portfolio investments which merely replace existing investments in this country and do not in any way add to the productive facilities of the country. The situation has now got to the point where in 1953 there was a productive investment of United States capital in Canada of some $8,600 million, of which a very large proportion, $4 billion, is in government and municipal bonds or other portfolio investments, none of which add directly to the expansion of our economy unless the sale of the government securities to such investors is then followed by a program of public investment in the country to expand these resources.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, in considering this whole problem of immigration we must also consider this problem of investment, and that we cannot much longer face the continued gradual decline in the volume of investment which has been reflected already in the rising level of unemployment. These things operate as immutably as night following day, but the way to deal with them is on a factual basis. I would suggest to the government also that there should be some fiscal discouragement of the investment of Canadian capital abroad while there is still so much to be done in expanding our facilities in Canada. I will not suggest what form this fiscal policy should take, but obviously it should be some sort of penalty that could be attached to capital investment abroad rather than in Canada. Perhaps there could be a withdrawal of the privilege that investors in Canadian companies now have, and that privilege should be confined to Canadian companies operating on the Canadian scene. If these measures fail, then I suggest that the government both for the sake of our present population and for the sake of ensuring our absorptive capacity of the volume of immigrants we all know this country requires, should undertake some balancing of the investment program on its own. I would add this, too. I agree with those speakers in the house who have pointed out that, to a certain degree, an increasing population brings with it expanding development in the way of production.
It was rather interesting to me to read the other day of a prominent industrialist who was pointing out that until our population is increased in Canada we cannot hope to engage

in large-scale mass production because we lack large-scale mass markets. Those are problems we should be facing.
And while the record of the administration of this department smells to high heaven and, in all kindness, I suggest to the minister to take his rose-coloured glasses off and get down to look at it-that's right: take them off-on the other hand I do hope that within a very short time he will be busily engaged in processing a much larger stream of immigrants so that neither he nor his subordinates will have time to play around with petty persecution, the record of which I have placed upon Hansard tonight.
Mr. Speaker, I come not as a stranger to a debate on immigration.
Mr. Speaker, I move that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) be now heard.
What about turn about in this business?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understood the hon. member for Spadina had been granted the floor by the Chair, and had already commenced his speech.
Carry on.

I am not sure that the hon. member for Kamloops was listening to me, so I shall commence again by saying that I come not as a stranger to a debate on immigration. Since coming to the House of Commons I have advocated immigration, in and out of season. When it was unpopular I attempted to popularize it, when it was popular I attempted to make it more so.
Unlike members of the house who have been quoting speeches others have made I have taken the trouble to read my own speeches on immigration, and I have found that from the time I came here in 1945 I have always been able to make at least one speech during a session on the subject of immigration. As I listened to the speeches made on Tuesday I thought I heard an echo, but with this difference, that my speeches were constructive.
I enter the debate for two special purposes. I feel the criticism of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who was the former minister of citizenship and immigration, is both unfair and unjustified. He deserves better from every section of the house. He took over and organized the department, and during the 10 years I have been in the house I have had some opportunity of judging his 50433-81
Immigration
administration. In my opinion it was excellent, by any standard. Surely in the last 10 years he has been by far the best immigration minister we have had.
Present company included?

I suggest that he was the first minister of citizenship and immigration who actually read and studied the regulations; and when he did, he changed the regulations so that at one time if you put pants on a penguin it could be admitted to this country. During the time he held the office three-quarters of a million people have come to this country as immigrants. That in itself is accomplishment enough for any one man.
I wish to say something about the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), who gave such an excellent account of himself this afternoon. We immigrants in the house have been educating him, and he is learning very quickly. In time he will do even better than he is doing now, because he has a sympathetic approach, understands the need, and is competent. At the present time he needs to be prodded a bit, because he is still a little timid. All we ask of him is a bold and courageous policy; we object to a stop and go policy with too many stops.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in his speech that two come in and one goes out. Others have spoken along the same line, but without elaborating. By that I gathered the hon. member meant that for every two immigrants coming in there is one emigrant who leaves the country.
We have talked a great deal about the immigrants who enter the country; I am going to speak for a few minutes about those who leave it, because they deserve a great deal more attention than they have received in the debate. This seems to be the appropriate occasion to discuss the matter. There has been reference during the course of the debate to the number of Canadians who have emigrated to the United States, and reference has been made particularly to skilled and professional people.
It has been very difficult for the government to pinpoint the cause of the emigration, except that we are all aware it has been going on for many years and, in the main, have attributed it to better salaries and greater opportunities in the United States. While that is far less true today than it used to be, it is still true. I have a case in point- and I do not hold the minister responsible for it, either.
Press reports indicate that the Medical Council of Canada has stated it will require medical graduates in Ontario and in some

Immigration
other provinces to serve in Canadian hospitals for at least one year of their internship before being licensed to practise. This proposed step to be taken by the medical council will surely increase and intensify the tide of emigration of the kind of people we can spare least.
These internes will continue to specialize in the United States, and abroad where more adequate facilities are available for advanced studies, at better wages and under better conditions, and more particularly where no comparable specialist facilities are available in Canada. These very same internes will be hesitant to return to Canada after the expiration of their internship in the United States to spend yet another year interning at low wages. They may have families and other obligations; they may have no other income. The consequence is that they will remain permanently in the United States.
It appears from everything I can gather that in Canada internes are paid as low as $10 and as high as $75 a month, with maintenance. Comparable wages in the United States, with maintenance, run from a low of $200 to a high of $300. Surely the time has come, if it is not long overdue, when the internes in Canada should be paid an existence wage and not be kept at servitude levels. This country will regret, and speaking for myself I now resent, the forcing of economic exile on many Canadians in whom we have large investments, both human and otherwise, for whom we have planned futures and who are urgently needed in this country to serve our own people.
The professional graduates of our universities, the engineers, the chemists, the doctors, the architects and others, are well aware of the opportunities that are available in the United States and abroad, but they are reluctant to leave Canada. They would much rather remain here but they are not prepared to sell their services at bargain prices. They ask to be paid salaries nearly comparable with those that are available in the United States and to be given comparable opportunities for advancement. According to press reports, 25 per cent of our medical graduates annually intern in the United States. What we need above all else is for the medical profession thoroughly to reexamine itself and its policies, because the Canadian people want to know why that is so. They are entitled to have an answer to why we are losing so many of our professional men in that field.
Policies such as I have indicated smack of compulsion. We do not like it; nor do we like the interference with personal liberty.

I close by saying that this has been a very useful debate. It has demonstrated, and it has been recorded, that all parties in this house are in favour of more and more immigration. That can be nothing less than an endorsation of the over-all government policy and the minister.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Spadina, who has just taken his seat, that this has been a very useful debate. It is the first opportunity we have had during the last three years to have a full discussion on the subject of immigration, and the house welcomes that opportunity.
As has been mentioned, last year's debate occurred on the last day of the session, on June 26, and it was a hurried affair which received somewhat scant attention. I spoke during that debate on June 26. I read over the Hansard of that day and discovered that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), then the minister of citizenship and immigration, although he had answered practically everyone else who had discussed items in his estimates, had failed to make any answer whatsoever to my statements. I had drawn attention to the fact that a major change of policy had occurred, in so far as I saw it, in the year 1949. I thought the minister would pay some attention to that, but he ignored it, or rather I should say he accepted my statement as being a correct interpretation of what had been going on.
In the course of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with one topic only tonight, namely, the long-term policy of immigration with respect to the ethnic basis of the population of Canada. In opening the debate on his amendment, the hon. member for Kamloops said, as reported at page 1158 of Hansard:
in the opinion of this house, the immigration policy of the government is not clear, consistent or co-ordinated; is not in conformity with the needs or the responsibilities of Canada; and in its administration denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike.
It is in connection with the first section of the amendment that I propose to deal. This afternoon the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration took the amendment in reverse order. He dealt at almost interminable length with the third section of it, touched on the middle section and ended to my surprise rather briefly on the first section and did not give a complete answer.
I would be glad to go on again if the hon. member would like me to.

I hope we shall be spared that fate. No doubt there will be a subsequent opportunity for the minister to participate again, and I hope that when his

estimates are under consideration he will reply to some of the remarks that I propose to make this evening.
On page 1163 of Hansard, in dealing with the question of the lack of clearness of government policy, the hon. member for Kamloops made this statement:
We do not say the immigration policy should lay undue or unfair emphasis on any one country at the expense of immigration from others. I repeat that we feel the country as a whole should pay a very real tribute to the contribution made to Canada by the people who have come to us from whatever country of origin.
Farther on he said:
Our criticism of the government in this sphere is that they have under-emphasized British immigration rather than that they have over-emphasized any other at the expense of British immigration.
In close connection with that I should like to quote a sentence or two from a speech made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) at page 1196, where he said:
On the subject of race I think the government owes a duty to the people of Canada to say, as we Conservatives say and say emphatically, that immigration into this country must never be permitted to have for its purpose disturbance of the fundamental racial position of Canada. We subscribe most emphatically to that point of view.
Some misunderstanding has been disclosed in the course of this debate as to what is the long-term policy of the government with regard to this question of the ethnic basis of our population. Tonight the minister made a correction when the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) was speaking and said that the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King had not laid it down that the policy envisaged no change in the ethnic basis of our population. There is a misunderstanding on the part of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais), who said at page 1185 of Hansard, quoting a statement that Mr. King had made in 1947:
Third, immigration should not be the cause of an undue change in the ethnical balance of the two main groups in this country.
If I heard him correctly tonight, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) repeated words to that effect. I had occasion to look at the statement that Mr. King made on May 1, 1947, to which frequent reference has been made today. Let us put it on the record so that we shall have it accurately. In the session of 1947, volume III, page 2646, we find the words of Mr. King, the then prime minister:
There will, I am sure, be general agreement with the view that the people of Canada do not wish, as a result of mass immigration, to make a fundamental alteration in the character of our population.
Immigration
I think that is the sentence around which this other statement has been built. When you read the rest of that statement of Mr. King's it is obvious that he was referring to mass immigration as being immigration from Asian countries. As I see it, there is nothing in his statement which would lead to the belief that he was concerned about the present ethnic basis of our population. Mark you, his sentences are sometimes subject to more meaning than one and even in that sentence there are plenty of escape routes had he been challenged with regard to immigration.
The words "mass immigration" would have lent themselves to considerable explanation. When does immigration become mass immigration? Is it at 10,000, or at 100,000 or at 1,000,000,000 a year? What do the words "character of our population" mean? It was drawn to our attention this afternoon that Mr. King was meticulous in his use of words and he must have suggested the word "character" for some particular purpose. It certainly has no connection with the racial origin of people in the country. It may refer to the peculiarities, characteristics or reputation of a nation but not to the ethnic division.
I have been asking this question for three years: What is the long-term policy with regard to immigration? The impression abroad is that the government is aiming its immigration policy to protect the basic ethnic divisions in this country, but at what stage do you start? Do you go back to confedera-*tion? Do you select the census of 1871? Do-you come to 1901, 1921 or the present period? There is quite a difference.
I should like to examine the formation of our population based on four large areas, the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario and the western provinces as indicated by information supplied by the department through the annual reports. I have worked out the following percentages in respect of the various races that comprise this country.
It is interesting to note that in 1871, the first census after confederation, the people of British origin in Canada were 60-55 per cent. According to the 1951 census they made up only 47-89 per cent of our population. In 1871 the French constituted 31-07 per cent of our population, and in 1951, 30-83 per cent. The great change occurred in the other racial groups which advanced from a percentage of 8-38 in 1871 to 21-28 in 1951. Therefore it is difficult to determine what is meant when people say that we are maintaining the fundamental racial position in Canada. Where is the point of departure?
Continuing that further and dealing with the various areas and the racial origins according to the census of 1951, in the Atlantic

Immigration
provinces the people of British Isles stock, whom I should like to term Anglo-Saxon, which would include British nationals who are here as immigrants and those who have been here as their descendants for years, constitute 71 per cent of the population. The French make up 20 per cent, while other racial groups make up 9 per cent.
In the province of Quebec the French constitute 83 per cent; the Anglo-Saxons 12 per cent; other racial groups 5 per cent.
In Ontario the Anglo-Saxons are 73 per cent of the population; the French, 11 per cent; others 16 per cent.
In the western provinces, Anglo-Saxons 60 per cent; French 7 per cent; others 33 per cent.
I should like to put on Hansard the figures of total population, which are as follows:
British stock or	Anglo-Saxons	 6,709,685
French origin	 4,319,167
Germanic and northern races of Europe
grouped together	 1,167,286
Slavic origin	 784,312
All others	 1,078,979
It is interesting to note that when you separate the people whose origin was the British Isles and those whose origin was France you have represented in Canada at least 39 other racial groups. As I have said before, as I said last year, and as I am happy to repeat at the present time, we welcome to this country people of various races. We have noted with interest the rapidity with which they become good Canadian citizens and we are proud of the contribution they have made toward building up this country.
Continuing the survey, I looked at the immigration figures for the last 50 years and gave them in the remarks I made in the house last year. As they failed to be noticed I think they are worthy of repetition on this occasion. I am going to give the immigration figures in 10-year periods from 1900 to 1954, excluding those who came from the United States. In the period 1900-09 approximately 60 per cent of the immigrants entering Canada were of of British stock with all others, we find that the report calls them. In the period 1910-19 they constituted 60 per cent; in the period 1920-29, 56 per cent; 1930-39, 45 per cent; 1940-49, 60 per cent.
Looking back at the immigration figures over a period of 50 years and comparing those of British stock with all others, we find that more than 50 per cent of the total number of immigrants entering Canada came from the British Isles. Contrast that with the situation over the last six years. Again I am quoting from the reports that the department publishes. In 1949 the people of British origin numbered 36 per cent of the total

immigrants entering this country. Again I am leaving out those from the United States. These figures are not for the calendar years. The department gives them by the fiscal year which ends on March 31. Hence it is March 31, 1949 that I am referring to. In that year 36 per cent of British stock entered this country as immigrants; in 1950, the figure was 25 per cent; in 1951, 20 per cent; in 1952, 17 per cent; in 1953, 29 per cent; and for the eleven months of 1954-the figure for which we have recently been given-29 per cent. The average for that almost six-year period comes to 26 per cent. Of the immigrants entering Canada 26 per cent were British nationals or of Anglo-Saxon stock.
My contention is that a definite change of policy occurred in the year 1949, and that change in policy seems to have been carried on through the years that have followed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who became minister of citizenship and immigration on January 18, 1950, must accept responsibility for that policy. It was not the policy in earlier days. As we all know, there was great immigration into Canada in the period from 1908 to 1914 under the governments of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden. Those were the years in which the western country was filled up; and we think of those years as being the great years of immigration into Canada. But when you examine the figures for the period from 1908 to 1914 you find that, of the total number of immigrants coming in at that time, the people of British stock were in the majority. On a percentage basis they were 61 per cent of those who came in at that time.
When did the change occur? A marked change was shown from 1949 on, but the first elements in the change became obvious about the year 1925; and during that period, 1926 to March 31, 1931-while a new government had come into power, the immigration policy could not be altered overnight-44 per cent of the immigrants entering Canada were of British origin. Even then there was some slight change in the ethnic basis of our population.
The point that I tried to make last year, and the point that I stress again on this occasion is this: Why this change from the earlier days with regard to our policy of immigration? What is the purpose behind it? What is the long-term policy of the government? Do the figures in the last six years indicate the policy of the government? Are they ignoring the ethnic groups who made up this country in the beginning? Are they indifferent to the nature of this country for the future?

An interesting article along that line appeared in the Canadian Legionary of January, 1953. The writer of the article was Mr. Edward H. Gurton who had been European commissioner of immigration for the Canadian National Railways, for many years western colonization manager of the C.N.R. and retired in 1950. In his article he draws attention to the decline in British immigration to Canada which, as I say, started in 1925 and has now become marked since 1949. He forecast the population changes that would occur if the present immigration policy was pursued to the end of this century. He suggested that, by the end of this century, there will be a marked difference in the racial composition of Canada. From page 7 I shall quote this paragraph:
Assuming that present trends continue, with no radical change to modify them, we appear to be destined to have, by the end of this century, a population whose racial origins will approximate:-
British	French	Others32%	30%	38%
It is even possible that, with continued large-scale immigration of its current character, and unless the proportion of British people in it can be increased substantially from the approximate 20 per cent of the last four years, we may reach A.D. 2000 with less than 30 per cent of our people of British racial stock.
In addition to other matters that have been drawn to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill) today with regard to the administration of his department, I think that this problem of long-term policy deserves the most serious and careful consideration. We have seen Canada develop successfully. We have been dependent upon immigration in order to offset the loss of our population to the United States. We have welcomed with open arms people from many nationalities and racial groups throughout the world. I speak not at all in the mood of an exclusionist. I think that Canada has gained a great deal from the special aptitudes and skills and the special cultures that various racial groups have brought to this country. But is there not some advantage in retaining the ethnic basis or something approaching the ethnic basis with which we started at confederation in 1867? Even if we retain it at the present figure, we must have some plan.
I fail to understand what the former minister of citizenship and immigration was intending in his policy which I could not get him to define last year. I fail to understand what the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is intending because he has not defined with any clarity the long-term policy of his department. I should like to point out that with all the assistance we have received from the 39 other racial groups
Immigration
that have come to this country, nevertheless Canada was explored and developed by the French and the Anglo-Saxons. The early settlement of the Atlantic provinces, the settlement and clearing of Ontario, the settlement of the western provinces, all these were done very largely by people of Anglo-Saxon origin. Although in the great migration of 1908 to 1914 others came who assisted, the western plains had already been opened up by people moving from other parts of Canada who cleared the ground, tilled the soil and established settlements.
We sometimes overlook the fact that the basic work of opening up this country was done by the two great basic stocks who originated the country. If we are looking for immigrants, as we are, what better place is there to look for them than the British Isles? The people of the British Isles over the centuries stand second to none as explorers and colonizers. Other racial groups have produced intrepid explorers, other racial groups have attempted colonization, but none has achieved results on such an impressive scale as the Anglo-Saxons. They are the world's foremost pioneers, the world's most successful colonizers. Wherever they have gone they have cleared the land, tilled the soil, planted crops and established settlements. The whole North American continent bears the marks of their genius for colonization.
In Canada, as I have mentioned, they were the ones who carved Ontario out of the wilderness. They developed the western plains and crossed the Rockies. Other racial groups have made effective contributions to the development of this dominion, but in most of our provinces the pioneering was commenced and settlements established by immigrants from the British Isles and their descendants.
Therefore I urge the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to take a second look at his policy and endeavour to attract to this country people from the British Isles in proportionate numbers to those who were attracted years ago. Why we should have reached the stage of receiving fewer people from the British Isles now than we did during the first 50 years of this century is not understandable at all.
In the last report of the department I notice that in their endeavour to obtain immigrants from the British Isles they have interviewed thousands of people there and on the continent other thousands. But let us take a comparison of the figures, and this is from page 29 of the department's report for 1954. They mention the fact that in the United Kingdom 202,551 office interviews were held and 49,863 medical cards were

Immigration
issued to British subjects, 24 per cent of those who were interviewed. On the continent of Europe they interviewed 284,000 people and issued 111,403 immigrant visas, 39 per cent of those who were interviewed on the continent.
I wonder why there should be that difference. I submit that the long-term policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is not clear, as has been stated in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I submit that the policy of May 1, 1947, as enunciated by the late Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, does not clearly establish that any attempt was being made then to maintain the racial groupings that were in effect in our country in the early days. I charge that from 1949 to the present time there has been a distinct change in the policy of immigration and that the emphasis has been on racial groups other than those from the British Isles. I think that a re-examination and a restatement of the long-term policy of immigration into Canada is desirable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to hon. members for entering this debate at this stage, but I believe that some of the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon make it necessary for me to speak and deal with what he had to say as briefly as I can. I noticed that the hon. member got quite a good hand from the members of his own group with a reference during his speech to an appeal to Caesar. While in my case he may not have appealed to Caesar I think that in his best courtroom manner he did qualify me as an expert witness to deal with what I took to be a very important element of the basis upon which he established or attempted to establish the criticisms that he levelled at the department of immigration and its procedures.
I think it must be clear to all hon. members that the hon. member for Prince Albert and also the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) built their case on grounds of their own choosing. They selected the grounds on which they sought to justify the statements they were making. I think it is also clear to all hon. members that the lack of validity and the weakness of their case can best be judged by the fact that to make that case the hon. member for Prince Albert had to resort to attempts to confuse and even to misrepresent the nature and contents of the material on which he based his case.
I refer in particular to what the hon. member had to say in connection with a subcommittee of the civil liberties section of the

Canadian Bar Association on which I served for two years. I also believe that we can be confident that the hon. member for Prince Albert has sufficient training and experience as a lawyer that he can be relied upon to produce the best evidence available to him to support a case, so that when he chooses to use inexact evidence not founded on fact this in itself proves with reasonable certainty that he did not have valid and sound evidence on which to base his statements.
The hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Kamloops referred to the subcommittee to which I have made reference and stated the date on which the subcommittee was established and the membership of the subcommittee. Thus far they were correct, but from there on I am afraid they part company with the truth. In the first place, the hon. member for Prince Albert described the subcommittee as a subcommittee set up to inquire into the immigration department and immigration matters in general. When he made that assertion he had available to him a wealth of evidence which proves conclusively that such a statement is not correct and, in fact, is completely misleading. For example, he had before him the terms of reference of the subcommittee which in part were as follows:
That a subcommittee on immigration be established to review the administration of immigration laws and regulations with particular reference to the curtailments of the rights of Canadians . . .
I believe that satisfactorily excludes matters of general immigration. In addition the chairman of the subcommittee in a public statement handed to the press I believe on September 4 in Winnipeg, and which received considerable publicity, had this to say:
It has not been the function of the committee to act as a board of inquiry. It has not been within the committee's terms of reference nor has it been the purpose of the individual members of the committee to consider matters of immigration policy. Throughout this work the committee has been concerned only with the rights of Canadian citizens, which stem from the Immigration Act, and in particular section 3, subsection 1 thereof, which states "a Canadian citizen has the right to come into Canada".
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Prince Albert completely confused himself and the house with respect to the report made by this subcommittee in September of this year. The report itself was put on the record by the minister this afternoon; that was the full report. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) in referring to the report mentioned criticism of the department and of government policy

which he said was implicit in this report. The minister, and I believe the minister is much more correct than the hon. member for Kamloops, labelled the report innocuous. He invited members opposite to show wherein it was critical.
Now, the hon. member for Prince Albert was not satisfied, as was the member for Kamloops, that criticism was implicit, and he attempted to comply with the invitation of the minister. He found he was unable to do so, and not being able to find justification in the report for the statements he was making, he went outside that report to other documents. He attempted to suggest, and even persisted under questioning by myself, that the documents to which he was referring formed a part of the report, and that these documents were accordingly made with the responsibility of the members of the committee. I state that any such impression is false and misleading. I propose to prove from the documents themselves that such an impression is false.
The hon. member for Prince Albert obviously had these documents in his possession when he was trying to create this impression. The text of the report itself which is before the house contains the following language, and I quote:
Mr. Taylor-
That is one of the members of the committee.
-has reviewed over 200 specific cases and has written four comprehensive reports on administrative procedures. These reports have been invaluable to the subcommittee and will form the basis for further study and representations. Copies of these reports are being filed with the chairman of the committee on civil liberties. However, the committee, and particularly Mr. Taylor, the author, believe that until such time as the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has had an opportunity of reviewing the detailed material contained in these reports, they should not be generally distributed.
That is what the report itself says with respect to the documents from which the hon. member for Prince Albert quoted while attempting to give the impression they were part of the report. Could anything, Mr. Speaker, be more clear than that these so-called reports were not part of the committee's report? The contents of these documents themselves further prove that the hon. member for Prince Albert really could not have misunderstood the situation. He had the reports. He waved them here in the house this afternoon.
Immigration
There are four of these reports and in paragraph 3 of the first one we find this:
This report is one of many to be submitted to the committee in order that the committee may draft a final report on the entire subject under review.
Each one of these documents contains a similar statement, and each of those documents is signed by one individual alone, Mr. John R. Taylor. I submit that these facts prove that the hon. member for Prince Albert had to go outside of the report to find any justification for the criticism that he was supposed to be basing on the subcommittee's report. I may say that these individual reports, in so far as they have been seen by me before they were filed with the committee chairman, were specifically and individually rejected by me as committee documents.
In so far as the report itself is concerned, and I would not deal with this except that I felt the hon. member for Prince Albert was laying some stress on the fact I had been a member of the committee, I saw a draft of a report which was sent to me by mail during the summer. I sent it back with corrections and suggestions about essential changes that should be made if any report were to be made.
I requested that if a report in final form were agreed upon it should be submitted to me before being filed or submitted to the committee on civil liberties. In fact, that was not done. The report was signed by the chairman himself, and in fairness to the chairman and to everybody else, it was clearly stated at the meeting of the Canadian Bar Association in Winnipeg that the report had been signed by the chairman only. Mr. Taylor was present to speak for himself; I was not present. I regarded this report, in so far as I saw it or had anything to do with drawing it up, as an interim report and I did not see the likelihood of it being put to political advantage. In that connection, apparently I forgot to consider the hon. member for Prince Albert.
The hon. member for Kamloops said that at Winnipeg the report became a hot political issue. I was not in Winnipeg, so I cannot judge except from what I am told. I understand one of the main causes for it becoming a hot political issue was that the hon. member for Prince Albert went out while the bar association convention was still going on and made a political speech at a political meeting based on the proceedings at the convention.

The hon. member no doubt knows that the deputy minister held a press conference in Winnipeg on the subject which was reported widely across Canada, long before there was any political meeting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I appreciate the consideration of hon. members so I shall finish what I have to say very quickly. As I was saying, to sum up this particular matter with respect to the report, the fact is, in so far as the hon. member for Prince Albert or anyone else attaches particular significance to it because of my name being attached to it- that is the only reason I mentioned the subject-I may say I did not see the final draft. It did not carry my approval in the form in which it appeared, nor did I sign it. I want to repeat that I repudiate absolutely the other documents from which the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) attempted to quote, for which I had no responsibility and which, in large part,
I had not even seen before they were filed.
Mr. Speaker, the final point with which I wish to deal-and I believe it is important that I do so-is in connection with the assertion that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) who was then minister of citizenship and immigration refused to see this subcommittee. That statement is not in the report; nor, so far as I can find or discover, is it in any document emanating from any member of the committee, either as a member of the committee or in his personal capacity.

This statement did appear in a press report as an unidentified statement, and it did not come to my attention until several weeks after the meeting in Winnipeg was over. When it did come to my attention I immediately got in touch with the chairman of the subcommittee to discover how that impression had been given, and to arrange for a public denial of it. Any suggestion that the then minister of citizenship and immigration refused to see the committee, or in any way obstructed the committee in what it wanted to do, is absolutely without foundation. The chairman of the committee, when I got in touch with him, advised me that he was as mystified as I was, and that he was unable to trace the source of the statement. Since then I have also been unable to trace the source of it. I repeat it is completely unfounded; and any suggestion by hon. members opposite that there is any truth in it is quite incorrect.
I think I should also say that the question of seeing the minister was purely informal. We were not in any sense authorized to wait upon the minister and speak for the Canadian Bar Association, or anything of that nature. It was purely a matter of courtesy, and an attempt by members of the committee to get reliable information, and to secure the co-operation of the minister and the department. I must say the minister made sure that that co-operation was forthcoming.
In conclusion I do think I should say that the Canadian Bar Association has a long history in the study of legislation #of this parliament and of the provinces, and of studying the conduct of government in the administration of justice, and many other important fields of governmental activity. Never before, so far as I know, has anything done by the Canadian Bar Association been used as a vehicle for political controversy or argument. I do not think it should have been used as a vehicle for political controversy or argument in this connection; and if I had any part or responsibility for bringing that about, I certainly am sincerely sorry.
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I appreciate the courtesy of the house in permitting me to finish, in a somewhat abbreviated form, the remarks I felt I should make, in the light of the quite unfounded and incorrect assertions the hon. member for Prince Albert included in his speech this afternoon.
On motion of Mr. Dinsdale the debate was adjourned.
